## 04. Problem Statement & Market Sizing

The preceding sections established *what* we build (filing-first, 20–200 employees) and *why the price floor is zero*. This section does the arithmetic underneath those decisions: it states the problem in the buyer's own terms, sizes the market on a denominator that survives audit, quantifies the money already being spent (from filed accounts, not analyst projections), and maps the competitive field to the one region where **obligation, budget and dissatisfaction overlap**. Every number here is either [Verified] against a primary source or carried as a [Hypothesis] with a named kill criterion. The banned figures from §20 — 6-crore MSMEs, $23.32bn, ₹83.3/USD, ₹37,500 CA fee — do not appear, and must not be reintroduced downstream.

A note on method before the argument. This section deliberately refuses two moves that every India-HR-tech deck makes. It does not quote a total-addressable-market number it cannot denominate, and it does not describe the product's advantage as a feature the incumbents lack (they lack none — they lack *execution and guarantee*). Both refusals cost us a bigger headline. Both are the reason the sizing survives a data room. Where a claim is load-bearing for the business case, it carries its provenance in line; where it is a placeholder, it carries the study that would collapse it to a point.

### 04.1 The problem, stated in the buyer's terms

The Indian employer of 20–200 people does not experience "HR software" as a category. They experience a recurring, dated, legally-enforced obligation to *file* — and a monthly scramble to get it right with tools and people that were never designed to file. Three distinct pains stack on top of each other, and the product's entire reason to exist is that it answers all three at once where the incumbents answer at most one.

#### Pain 1 — The statutory burden is a step function that gets worse as you grow

Indian labour and tax compliance is not a flat cost; it turns on at headcount thresholds, and each threshold adds a new *filing* with its own portal, format, cadence and penalty regime. The beachhead employer sits squarely inside the zone where the burden compounds.

| Headcount | Obligation that turns on | Filing artefact | Cadence | Penalty exposure for getting it wrong |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | TDS u/s 192; Shops & Establishments; minimum wages; prescribed-format appointment letter (new since 21 Nov 2025) | Form 138 (ex-24Q); Form 130 (ex-Form 16) | Quarterly + annual | Interest u/s 201; late-filing fee ₹200/day u/s 234E [Verified] |
| 10 | ESI; gratuity accrual; maternity benefit ("on any day of preceding 12 months" — latches once crossed) | ESI challan; ESI returns | Monthly + half-yearly | ESI damages up to 25% p.a. of arrears; interest at 12% p.a. [Verified — ESIC Regs; exact damages slab to reconfirm against current ESIC (General) Regulations] |
| 20 | **EPF**; grievance redressal committee | ECR; PF Forms 3A/5/6A/10/12A | Monthly by the 15th | 14B damages (5–25% p.a. by delay slab) + 7Q interest at 12% p.a. [Verified — EPF Scheme framework] |
| 50 | Crèche facility | — | — | Directions under the Codes |
| 100 | Works committee | — | — | Directions under the Codes |
| 300 | Retrenchment/closure approval (raised from 100 by the new Codes) | Government approval | Event-driven | Order invalid without approval [Verified] |

(Source: Code on Social Security 2020 and Central Rules notified 8 May 2026; Income-tax Act s.192/234E; consistent with PRD §6.)

Behind each threshold sits an actual contribution or benefit computation, and the *numbers* are where a spreadsheet or an inattentive bureau quietly goes wrong. The mechanics that the payroll engine must get right, deterministically, every period:

| Levy | Rate / formula | Wage base & ceiling | Edge cases the engine must handle | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **EPF** | 12% employee + 12% employer | Statutory ceiling ₹15,000/mo; of the employer 12%, **8.33% routes to EPS capped at ₹15,000 (= ₹1,250)**, remainder to EPF | International workers have **no ceiling**; employer may voluntarily contribute on actuals above ₹15,000; PF wages redefined by the 50% add-back (below) | EPF Scheme 1952 / Scheme 2026; EPS 1995 [Verified — framework; migrate to Scheme 2026 per PRD §6] |
| **EDLI** | 0.5% employer | On EPF wages, ceiling ₹15,000 | Exemption route where a group insurance scheme is in force (Form 5(IF) on death) | EDLI 1976 [Verified — framework] |
| **EPF admin** | 0.5% employer (min charge applies) | On EPF wages | Zero for exempted establishments | EPFO admin charge notification [Hypothesis — minimum-charge rupee floor to reconfirm] |
| **ESI** | 0.75% employee + 3.25% employer | Gross wages, ceiling **₹21,000/mo** (₹25,000 for persons with disability) | Wage crossing the ceiling **mid-contribution-period** does not stop ESI until the period (Apr–Sep / Oct–Mar) ends; ₹0-wage days | ESI (Central) Amendment Rules 2019; ESIC [Verified — rate cut effective 1 Jul 2019] |
| **Gratuity** | (last-drawn wages × 15 × completed years) ÷ 26 | "Wages" per the Code; cap **₹20 lakh** | **5-year continuous service** eligibility waived pro-rata for fixed-term employees under the Codes; gratuity base rises under the add-back | Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 → Code on Social Security 2020 [Verified — framework; ₹20L cap to reconfirm] |
| **Bonus** | 8.33%–20% of eligible wages | Eligibility wage ≤ ₹21,000/mo; calc ceiling ₹7,000 or minimum wage, whichever higher | Set-on/set-off of allocable surplus across years; new/loss-making units | Payment of Bonus Act 1965 → Code on Wages 2019 [Verified — framework] |
| **Maternity** | 26 weeks paid (first two children; 12 weeks thereafter) | Average daily wage | Applies at 10+ employees; crèche at 50; work-from-home post-leave by agreement | Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act 2017 → Code on Social Security [Verified] |

Three consequences follow, each of which the product must answer:

- **The problem is not "run payroll" — it is "produce and lodge a correct return, on time, on a government portal, every month, forever."** ICAI's own recommended fee schedule confirms the buyer's mental model: it prices TDS return filing, PT registration and PT returns — and has **no line item for "payroll processing" at all** [Verified, PRD §18]. The unit of value the market already pays for is the filing.
- **The burden is dated and unforgiving.** EPF ECR is due monthly by the 15th; PT returns are state-specific and range monthly to annual; TDS is quarterly with a shifting file format (Form 138 replaced 24Q; the Q4 regular format did not exist as of the research date — PRD §6). A missed deadline is not a soft failure; it is interest, damages and, for TDS, disallowance of expenditure.
- **The burden is multiplying under transition.** Four Labour Codes in force 21 Nov 2025; Central Rules 8 May 2026; a one-year saving of EPF/ESI schemes expiring ~21 Nov 2026; the "50% wages add-back" creating **two concurrent wage bases on one payslip** (PRD §6). The employer who was compliant last year is not automatically compliant this year — and cannot know it without a maintained system.

##### Worked example — the 50% add-back, in rupees

The hardest single calculation in the build (PRD §6) is abstract until you run one payslip through it. Take a ₹50,000/month employee at a beachhead firm with a typical CTC split:

| Component | Monthly ₹ | Counts as "wages"? (Code on Wages s.2(y)) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basic | 15,000 | Yes |
| HRA | 7,500 | Excluded |
| Conveyance | 1,600 | Excluded |
| Special allowance | 22,000 | Excluded |
| LTA | 2,000 | Excluded |
| Wages (pre add-back) | **15,000 (30%)** | — |
| Excluded total | **35,000 (70%)** | — |

The proviso: where the excluded components exceed **one-half of total remuneration**, the excess over one-half is *deemed wages and added back*. Half of ₹50,000 is ₹25,000; excluded is ₹35,000; the excess is **₹35,000 − ₹25,000 = ₹10,000**. Post add-back, wages = ₹15,000 + ₹10,000 = **₹25,000** (exactly 50% of remuneration).

Downstream effect on the same payslip:

- **Gratuity base** (uncapped by any ₹15,000 ceiling) jumps from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 — a **66% rise in accrued gratuity liability** per employee, applied retrospectively once the rule bites.
- **PF base**: if the employer contributes only to the ₹15,000 ceiling, PF is unchanged; but if the employer already contributes on actual basic (common above the ceiling), the base rises from ₹15,000 to ₹25,000 and monthly PF cost rises with it. The engine must know *which policy each tenant runs*.
- **Two wage bases now coexist on one payslip**: the add-back base (₹25,000, excludes HRA/conveyance/OT/bonus) drives PF and gratuity; the payment-of-wages / equal-remuneration base (₹50,000, includes them) drives minimum-wage and overtime tests. A single "salary" field cannot represent both.
- The statute says "or such other per cent as may be notified" — 50% is a **standing variable, not a constant** (PRD §6). The rule must be effective-dated and retrospectively recomputable.

##### Worked examples — the four other levies where the number quietly goes wrong

The add-back is the hardest single calculation, but it is not the only one where a spreadsheet accrues silent liability. Four more, each run in rupees on the same 60-person beachhead firm, because "the rule is subtle" only lands when you watch it break a real payslip.

**(a) ESI contribution-period continuity — the mid-period crossing (AC-4).** ESI contribution periods are fixed: April–September and October–March. Eligibility is tested at the *start* of the period; once a member is in, a mid-period pay rise does not drop them. Take an employee at ₹20,500 gross in April (below the ₹21,000 ceiling, so ESI applies). They get a raise to ₹24,000 effective 1 July.

| Month | Gross | Naive tool ("stop at ceiling") | Correct (ESIC rule) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Apr–Jun | 20,500 | ESI on 20,500 | ESI on 20,500 |
| Jul–Sep | 24,000 | **ESI dropped** (over ₹21k) | **ESI continues on 24,000** until 30 Sep |
| Oct onward | 24,000 | — | Now genuinely out; drops from new period |

A tool that drops the member on the July crossing under-remits three months of ESI (employee 0.75% + employer 3.25% on ₹24,000 = **₹960/month × 3 = ₹2,880** short), and — worse — the *employee* is wrongly shown as uncovered mid-treatment, creating benefit-denial liability on the employer. The engine must contribute on the *actual* (raised) wage for the rest of the period, not freeze at ₹21,000. (Source: ESI (Central) Rules, contribution-period rule; ESIC [Verified — period structure]; exact "continue on raised wage" treatment to reconfirm against current ESIC instructions [Hypothesis].)

**(b) Gratuity accrued liability — the add-back applied across tenure.** The add-back's ₹15,000→₹25,000 base jump (above) is a per-employee balance-sheet event, not a payslip line. Gratuity = (last-drawn wages × 15 × completed years) ÷ 26, capped ₹20 lakh. For a 7-year employee:

| Wage base | Per-year accrual (base × 15 ÷ 26) | Accrued at 7 years |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ₹15,000 (pre add-back) | ₹8,654 | ₹60,577 |
| ₹25,000 (post add-back) | ₹14,423 | ₹1,00,962 |

The add-back lifts this one employee's accrued gratuity liability by **₹40,385 (≈67%)**, and it applies to *every* employee whose structure trips the 50% test — a step-change in the firm's Ind AS 19 / actuarial provision the month the rule bites, recognised retrospectively. A payroll tool that treats gratuity as a payslip afterthought misses a liability the auditor will not. (Source: Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 s.4 → Code on Social Security 2020; ₹20L cap [Verified — framework; cap to reconfirm].)

**(c) Professional Tax — Maharashtra's February top-up.** Maharashtra caps PT at the constitutional ₹2,500/year (Art. 276) but collects it as **₹200 × 11 months + ₹300 in February** for salaries above the top slab. An engine that hard-codes a flat ₹200/month remits ₹2,400/year — **₹100 short of the ₹2,500 cap**, every year, per employee. Across 40 above-slab employees that is ₹4,000/year of quiet under-remittance plus interest, and it is a documented recurring engine-bug source precisely because the February value is an exception, not a slab. The two-part logic (11 × ₹200 + 1 × ₹300) must be a rule, not a constant. (Source: Maharashtra State Tax on Professions, Trades, Callings and Employments Act 1975; constitutional cap Art. 276(2) [Verified — cap]; the ₹200/₹300 split [Hypothesis — reconfirm against current MH schedule, PRD §13].)

**(d) Statutory bonus — the ₹7,000 calc ceiling and set-on/set-off.** The Payment of Bonus Act (→ Code on Wages) makes employees earning ≤ ₹21,000/month *eligible*, but computes the bonus on a *capped* base of **₹7,000/month or the applicable minimum wage, whichever is higher** — not on actual salary. For an eligible employee at ₹18,000/month in a state where the scheduled minimum wage for their category is ₹10,500:

- Calc base = max(₹7,000, ₹10,500) = **₹10,500**, not ₹18,000.
- At the statutory floor of 8.33%: annual bonus = ₹10,500 × 12 × 8.33% = **₹10,496**; at the 20% ceiling (when allocable surplus permits): **₹25,200**.

A tool that pays 8.33% of *actual* ₹18,000 over-remits by ~71%; one that uses a bare ₹7,000 floor and ignores a higher minimum wage under-remits. The rate between 8.33% and 20% is not a constant either — it is driven by *set-on / set-off of allocable surplus* carried across up to four years, so a loss-making beachhead unit in its formative years and a profitable one owe different percentages on the same salary. (Source: Payment of Bonus Act 1965 s.10–12, s.15 → Code on Wages 2019 [Verified — framework]; minimum-wage linkage [Verified — statutory]; per-state minimum-wage schedules [Hypothesis].)

The through-line across all four: none of these is a "salary × rate" one-liner. Each has a ceiling, an exception, or a cross-period carry that a flat spreadsheet formula gets wrong in the direction of silent under- or over-remittance — and each is invisible until an inspection, an actuarial valuation, or an employee grievance surfaces it. This is the concrete content of "the filing, not the payslip, is the unit of delivery."

##### The edge cases that manufacture retro-liability

Beyond the headline levies, a cluster of threshold-and-eligibility edge cases is where a spreadsheet or an inattentive bureau accrues silent liability. These are not exotic — they occur in ordinary beachhead firms every year.

| Edge case | Rule | Why it bites in the beachhead | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PoSH Internal Committee | Mandatory at **10+ employees** | Latches at the same headcount as ESI/gratuity; often missed as a "non-payroll" obligation | Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013 [Verified — threshold] |
| Fixed-term employee gratuity | 5-year continuous-service bar **waived pro-rata** under the Codes | Common in the beachhead's project/contract staffing; accrual starts from year one | Code on Social Security 2020 [Verified — framework] |
| Apprentices | Excluded from PF/ESI while under the Apprentices Act | Mis-classifying an apprentice as an employee over-remits; the reverse under-remits | Apprentices Act 1961 [Verified — framework] |
| International workers | **No EPF wage ceiling** — contribution on full pay | A single expat/returning-NRI hire breaks the ₹15,000-ceiling assumption | EPF Scheme, IW provisions [Verified — framework] |
| Contract labour | Principal-employer liability for PF/ESI if the contractor defaults | The beachhead firm inherits the contractor's non-compliance | Contract Labour (R&A) Act / Code on OSH [Verified — principal-employer principle] |
| Arrears / retro wage revision | Recompute PF/ESI/PT/TDS against the **period's** rule version | Add-back and slab changes make retro runs non-trivial (AC-2) | Code on Wages; EPF Scheme [Verified — principle] |
| LWF employer/employee split | Differs by state, remitted monthly/half-yearly/annually | Tiny rupees, many distinct rules — a maintenance load, not a calculation one | State LWF Acts [Hypothesis — per-state amounts] |

The through-line: each of these is a place where "run payroll" and "file correctly, provably, forever" diverge — and each is invisible until an inspection or an employee grievance surfaces it. The audit trail (AC-9) and effective-dated recompute (AC-2) exist precisely to make these defensible rather than discovered.

Two of these edge cases are worth a rupee illustration, because their *shape* — not their magnitude — is what defeats a spreadsheet:

- **International worker, PF uncapped.** A returning-NRI hire at ₹2,00,000/month is an "international worker" with **no ₹15,000 ceiling**: PF is computed on full pay. Employee 12% + employer 12% on ₹2,00,000 = **₹48,000/month** of PF, against the ₹3,600 a ceiling-capped domestic employee at the same salary would show — a **13.3× difference on one payslip**. A tool that applies the ₹15,000 ceiling universally under-remits ₹44,400/month for this one worker and mislabels their contribution class on the ECR. The engine needs a per-employee IW flag that overrides the tenant-level ceiling policy (AC-5), not a global constant. (Source: EPF Scheme, International Worker provisions, para 83 [Verified — no-ceiling principle]; exact wage definition for IWs to reconfirm.)
- **LWF, the many-tiny-rules problem.** LWF is a few rupees, but the *rules* are the cost. Illustrative shape across three states for a single employee: one state deducts ₹25 employee + ₹50 employer *half-yearly*; another ₹20 + ₹40 *annually in December*; a third a monthly ₹6 + ₹12. Total annual employer outlay for this employee across all three: under ₹250. Yet each has a different amount, split, month and portal — so a three-state firm carries three independent LWF cadences that a "flat monthly ₹X" formula cannot represent, and a missed December-annual remittance is a compliance flag for the sake of ₹40. This is the canonical "maintenance load, not calculation load" (PRD §13): trivial rupees, non-trivial *rule count*. (Source: respective State LWF Acts [Hypothesis — all per-state amounts, splits and cadences pending the gazette dataset, PRD §13/§20]; that LWF is a state subject with divergent cadence [Verified as structural].)

##### Worked example — TDS's breaking file-format change

The TDS filing is not a stable target the buyer can "set and forget" — it is actively breaking underneath them this year, which is why a *maintained* system beats a spreadsheet macro that encoded last year's layout. Form 138 replaces 24Q and the record layout is a breaking change, not a rename (PRD §6):

| What changed | Old (24Q) | New (Form 138) | Consequence for the filer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Challan sub-headings | 301–312 | Remap to A–K, **303 deleted** | Any tool hard-coding challan codes emits an invalid file |
| Annexure I fields | 313–327 | Remap to C–N, with **313, 321, 322, 325 removed** | Field-position parsers break silently |
| Surcharge / Education Cess / Penalty-Others | Present | **Deleted** | Amounts that used to have a home now have none |
| Interest Allocation / Others Allocation | Absent | **Added** | New mandatory fields a stale template does not populate |
| Rollout | — | Q1–Q3 v1.2 shipped 22 Jul 2026; correction-statement structures 4 Aug 2026 | Mid-year format churn |
| **Q4 regular format** | — | **Does not exist yet** as of research | Form 130 (ex-Form 16) Part B cannot be fully built until it lands |

(Source: NSDL/Protean file-format releases, 2026; PRD §6. [Verified].)

The buyer-facing point: an employer running a spreadsheet or an un-maintained tool cannot even *know* their Q1 2026 return format is stale until TRACES rejects it — and the Q4/Form 130 dependency means the annual certificate is blocked on a format that has not shipped. This is precisely the "maintained updates" value that Tally's ₹0-incremental licence and Frappe's OSS model cannot contractually guarantee (PRD §5, §13). It is also a concrete instance of the standing rule: a watcher keyed only to *new instruments* would miss a corrigendum to the *format*, exactly the failure mode that inverted the November 2026 analysis (PRD §2).

##### Worked example — the mid-year joiner and previous-employer income

The single most common TDS defect in the beachhead is not the file format — it is the mid-year joiner whose previous-employer income and TDS are not picked up. Take an employee who joins the 60-person firm on 1 October with a ₹9,00,000/year package, having earned ₹4,50,000 and suffered ₹18,000 TDS at their prior employer in Apr–Sep.

- **If the new employer ignores the prior income** (the spreadsheet default): it deducts TDS as though annual income were ₹4,50,000 (Oct–Mar only) — landing the employee near the exemption/lower-slab boundary and **under-deducting** for the year.
- **The correct treatment (s.192(2), Form 12B):** the employee furnishes prior salary and TDS on Form 12B; the new employer aggregates ₹4,50,000 + ₹4,50,000 = ₹9,00,000, computes tax on the *whole*, credits the ₹18,000 already deducted, and deducts the balance rateably over Oct–Mar.

At ₹9 lakh under the new regime, aggregate liability is materially higher than the sum of two "half-year" computations because the slabs are annual and progressive. The gap surfaces only in the employee's own Form 130 (ex-Form 16) reconciliation or an intimation u/s 143(1) — by which point it is the *employee's* refund shortfall and the *employer's* short-deduction exposure u/s 201. The engine must (i) accept Form 12B prior-income input at onboarding, (ii) annualise on aggregate, and (iii) reconcile prior-employer TDS credit — none of which a single-employer salary column can represent. This is exactly one of the "judgement calls the bureau carries" (Pain 3) made visible and deterministic. (Source: Income-tax Act s.192(2); Rule 26A / Form 12B [Verified — framework]; new-regime slabs per Finance Act in force [Verified as structural].)

##### The November 2026 cliff as a market-timing wedge

One statutory fact does double duty as a *sizing* argument, not just an engineering one. The EPF Act 1952 is repealed with effect from 21 Nov 2025; Code on Social Security s.164(2)(b) saves the EPF/EDLI/EPS schemes and all ESI rules for *one year*, expiring ~**21 Nov 2026** (PRD §6, [Verified]). The EPF side has a named successor (Employees' Provident Funds Scheme, 2026, 12% re-notified retrospectively by S.O. 3582(E)); **the ESI side is unresolved**.

Why this matters to the market, not just the codebase:

- It creates a **forced re-evaluation moment** across the entire contributing base simultaneously. Every 20–200 employer must confirm their payroll runs against Scheme 2026 and whatever replaces the ESI saving — a rare synchronous trigger in a market where switching inertia is otherwise the dominant force (§04.2).
- It is a **wedge against the status quo specifically**. A Tally-plus-CA arrangement survives on the CA quietly absorbing changes; a cliff of this size, with an *unresolved ESI leg*, is exactly the kind of event where the black-box relationship (Pain 3) fails visibly and the employer starts shopping.
- It is **time-boxed**, which is unusual and valuable for GTM. The window in which "are you ready for 22 November 2026?" is a live buyer anxiety is measured in months, and it maps to the §20 (V-08) primary-source watch.

> [Hypothesis] The cliff is a launch-timing tailwind, not just a compliance risk.
> **Kill criterion:** if ESIC re-notifies its schemes cleanly and early (well before 21 Nov 2026) with no disruption, the "forced re-evaluation" tailwind weakens to the ordinary annual-Budget change cadence, and acquisition timing loses this specific hook.

##### Why now — three timing forces converge on the launch window

The cliff is one of three near-simultaneous forces that make the 12–18 months from the research date an unusually good entry window. None is individually decisive; together they compress the market's ordinary switching inertia.

| Force | Nature | Timing | Direction on entry |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nov 2026 EPF/ESI cliff | Regulatory (forced re-check) | ~21 Nov 2026, ESI leg unresolved | Tailwind — synchronous re-evaluation (above) |
| Four Codes + Central Rules bedding in | Regulatory (new spec) | In force 21 Nov 2025; Rules 8 May 2026; state rules rolling unevenly | Tailwind — "build against a settled spec" (PRD §6), and every employer's prior config is now suspect |
| Zoho free-gate widening | Competitive (price floor moves) | Unknown date; treated as *when*, not *if* (PRD §18, §16) | Headwind — compresses the paid floor from below |

The read: the two regulatory forces open a window in which "is your payroll correct under the new regime?" is a live, dated anxiety the incumbent Tally-plus-CA arrangement answers opaquely — and the competitive force sets a clock on how long the 20–50 sub-band stays monetisable before Zoho zero-prices it. A filing-first entrant wants to land *while both regulatory triggers are fresh and before the free floor widens*, which is the concrete GTM meaning of the beachhead being "over-served by cheap product, under-served by product that files" (PRD §1).

> [Hypothesis] The regulatory tailwind outweighs the Zoho-gate headwind for a launch inside this window.
> **Kill criterion:** if Zoho (or a fintech, PRD §16) widens the free gate to 50 *before* the regulatory re-check anxiety converts pipeline, the entry window closes on the lower beachhead and the launch must re-center on 50–200 at higher PEPM — the §04.3 grid re-run on the upper sub-band (see §04.4 structural risks).

##### Acceptance criteria — Pain 1 (statutory engine)

These are the pass/fail tests the engine must meet for this section's thesis to hold. They are written so a §20 prototype can be graded against them.

- **AC-1 (dual wage base).** For any CTC structure, the engine computes and stores at least two concurrent wage bases per employee per period; a change to the add-back percentage re-derives both without manual re-entry.
- **AC-2 (effective-dated rules).** A retro/arrears run for period *P* recomputes against the rule version in force *for P*, not the version in force today, and emits an audit trail showing which version applied. (Directly mirrors PRD §6.)
- **AC-3 (deterministic statutory numbers).** No PF/ESI/PT/TDS/gratuity figure is ever model-generated; the LLM may explain a number but never produce one (PRD §8, "rules-first, LLM-last").
- **AC-4 (contribution-period continuity).** An ESI member whose wage crosses ₹21,000 mid-period continues to contribute until the contribution period closes; the engine does not drop them at the crossing.
- **AC-5 (ceiling policy per tenant).** PF is computed on either the ₹15,000 ceiling or actual wages per a tenant-level policy flag, and the two never silently diverge across employees.
- **AC-6 (Scheme 2026 migration).** All EPF computation references the Employees' Provident Funds Scheme, 2026, not the repealed 1952 Scheme, and carries a corrigendum-check flag per the standing rule (PRD §2).

The four worked examples above add four more pass/fail tests, sub-lettered so they do not renumber AC-7 onward:

- **AC-4a (ESI raised-wage continuity).** When an in-period ESI member's wage rises above ₹21,000, the engine contributes on the *raised actual* wage for the remainder of the contribution period, not on the frozen ₹21,000 ceiling and not zero.
- **AC-6a (gratuity as a liability, not a payslip line).** Every add-back or wage revision re-derives per-employee accrued gratuity on the correct base and surfaces the aggregate liability delta for actuarial/provisioning use — retrospectively for the affected period.
- **AC-6b (bonus calc ceiling + minimum-wage floor).** Statutory bonus is computed on max(₹7,000, applicable minimum wage), never on actual salary, with the 8.33%–20% rate driven by set-on/set-off carried across up to four years — not a hard-coded 8.33%.
- **AC-6c (PT exception months).** State PT is a rule table with per-month exceptions (e.g. Maharashtra's ₹300 February top-up to hit the ₹2,500 cap), never a flat monthly constant; annual PT reconciles to the state cap per employee.
- **AC-6d (mid-year joiner aggregation).** The engine accepts Form 12B prior-employer income and TDS at onboarding, annualises tax on the aggregate, and credits prior TDS — no single-employer-only TDS run for a mid-year joiner.

#### Pain 2 — The tooling is fragmented, and the seams are where errors live

The 20–200 employer does not run one system. They run a *stack of partial systems joined by spreadsheets and manual re-keying*, and every join is a place a statutory number goes wrong.

| Function | What the beachhead employer typically uses today | The seam / failure mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Payroll calculation | Tally payroll module, or Excel, or a CA's in-house tool | Wage-base definitions not versioned; add-back rule applied inconsistently |
| Attendance | eSSL/ZKTeco biometric terminal + its own time-office software | Punch data manually exported and re-keyed into payroll; OT ceiling (144 hrs/quarter) untracked |
| Statutory filing | CA/bureau logs into EPFO/ESIC/TRACES/state PT portals | No single source of truth; the employer cannot see filing status until something breaks |
| Employee queries | Email, WhatsApp, HR person's memory | Payslip disputes, investment declarations, Form 16 requests all manual |
| Records | Paper registers or per-portal downloads | Four consolidated statutory registers (electronic, 5-yr retention) not maintained as a system |

The cost of fragmentation is not licence fees — it is **re-keying error, reconciliation labour, and the absence of a defensible audit trail**. This is the specific gap the PRD's positioning attacks: not feature parity with Zoho (that is table stakes, PRD §5), but *filing-as-a-service over a single record*, which Tally structurally cannot do and a spreadsheet-plus-CA arrangement does badly.

Two seams are worth naming concretely because they are the highest-frequency error sources in the beachhead:

- **The attendance→payroll seam.** A biometric terminal records punches; those punches must become paid days, overtime hours (capped at 144/quarter per worker — PRD §9), leave deductions and loss-of-pay. When this crosses a manual export, OT is mis-stated, the 144-hour ceiling is invisible, and the wage base for PF/ESI is wrong before any filing runs. The device push receiver (ADMS/WDMS, PRD §9) exists to close exactly this seam without middleware.
- **The wage-master→filing seam.** The ECR, ESI challan and PT return each need the *same* employee master with *different* wage definitions (add-back base for PF, gross for ESI, salary slab for PT). A spreadsheet keeps one column called "salary" and derives the rest by hand. Every derivation is a defect opportunity.

##### Acceptance criteria — Pain 2 (single record, closed seams)

- **AC-7 (one master, many views).** ECR, ESI challan, PT return and TDS annexure all draw from one employee/wage master; no filing is produced by re-keying from another artefact.
- **AC-8 (attendance closes into payroll).** Punch data from a supported device (eSSL/ZKTeco via ADMS push) resolves to paid days, OT (with 144-hr/quarter guardrail) and LOP with no manual export step.
- **AC-9 (audit trail).** Every statutory figure is traceable to the source record and rule version that produced it, satisfying the four consolidated registers with five-year electronic retention (PRD §14).

#### Pain 3 — The bureau relationship is a real, recurring budget line — and a black box

The dominant "solution" in the beachhead today is not software. It is a **CA or payroll bureau** charging a monthly retainer to run the filings and carry the judgement calls. This is simultaneously the incumbent to displace-or-partner-with and the price anchor for everything.

- Verified anchor: bureaus charge roughly **₹3,000–15,000/month** for the beachhead (PRD §5). At the low end that is ~₹36k/year; at the high end ~₹1.8L/year — a meaningful, defensible budget line that already exists and does not need to be created.
- The black-box problem: the employer pays the retainer but has **no visibility into filing status, no self-serve record, and single-person key risk** (the relationship lives in the CA's head and login). When the CA is slow, sick, or wrong, the *employer* carries the statutory liability — the notice from EPFO or the AO lands on the *employer*, not the bureau.
- The judgement calls the bureau carries — the add-back interpretation, which allowances count as PT-liable, whether a mid-year joiner's previous-employer TDS is picked up — are precisely the calls that a maintained rules engine can standardise and make visible. Today they are opaque even to the employer paying for them.

> [Hypothesis] The realised bureau price is the single most important unvalidated number in the entire market model.
> If a CA in a Class-B city actually charges under ₹2,000/month for 20–50 people, the ₹80–150 PEPM anchor (PRD §18) collapses and the beachhead economics must be rebuilt.
> **Kill criterion:** mystery-shop 6–8 CAs/bureaus across two city tiers for 20/50/100-person quotes (PRD §20, V-01). If the median monthly quote is < ₹2,000, re-anchor pricing before any funding decision.

**Where the three pains converge is the beachhead thesis:** the 20–200 employer has a *legally-enforced, dated obligation* (Pain 1), *fragmented tooling that manufactures errors* (Pain 2), and *an existing budget line paid to a black box* (Pain 3). That is obligation + dissatisfaction + budget in one segment — the definition of a market.

#### Who actually buys — the decision anatomy of a beachhead firm

Market sizing is meaningless without knowing who inside a 60-person firm signs, who uses, and who the product must *not* alienate. The beachhead buying unit is small and unusual — the same person often occupies three of these roles, and the external CA is inside the loop.

| Role | Who it is in a 20–200 firm | What they care about | Implication for the product |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Economic buyer | Founder / owner / CFO | The penalty notice lands on *them*; wants the retainer line controlled | Sell on liability removal and visibility, not features |
| Admin user | One HR/admin person (often <1 FTE on HR) | Not being blamed when a filing is late; not re-keying | Filing-status dashboard; single record (AC-7) |
| The CA / bureau | External, part-time, holds the portal logins | Their retainer, their judgement calls, their client relationship | Channel, not enemy — CA console (PRD §18), or they block the sale |
| Employees | 20–200 people | Payslip, Form 16, investment declaration, leave balance | Employee/mobile surface — the thing Tally lacks (PRD §5) |

Two consequences for GTM and therefore for CAC:

- **The CA is a gatekeeper, not a bystander.** In many beachhead firms the CA *is* the person who would evaluate and recommend the software, because the founder delegates compliance entirely. A product that reads as "disintermediate your CA" gets vetoed by the one person the founder trusts on this. This is why "design for the CA as a user" is the most consequential GTM call in the PRD — and why it is also entirely unvalidated (PRD §18, §20 V-05). If CAs see us as a threat, the channel inverts into an opponent and CAC rises.
- **The admin user has almost no time budget.** HR is a fractional job in a 60-person firm. The buyer will not sit through an enterprise demo cycle, which is the concrete reason self-serve INR pricing and a published price card are table stakes (AC-14, PRD §18), not polish.

> [Hypothesis] The CA is a channel, not a competitor, in the beachhead buying unit.
> **Kill criterion:** 20–30 practising-CA interviews across two city tiers (PRD §20 V-05). If CAs predominantly see filing-first software as disintermediation of their retainer, the primary GTM motion is wrong and must flip to direct-to-founder with the CA as an integration, not a channel.

#### The status-quo alternatives the buyer weighs

The competitor at the point of sale is rarely another SaaS — it is the arrangement the firm already runs. Naming the real alternatives is what keeps the wedge honest (it is *quality-of-delivery*, not *availability* — PRD §1).

| Status-quo option | What it costs the buyer today | Where it fails the buyer | Why we win / why we do not |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Excel + in-house | ~₹0 licence; heavy hidden labour + error risk | No audit trail; add-back and TDS-format changes silently break it | Win on correctness + maintained updates |
| TallyPrime + CA | ₹0-incremental licence + ₹3k–15k/mo retainer | No filing-as-a-service, no employee surface, no status visibility | Win on execution, surfaces, visibility (PRD §5) |
| Pure bureau (no software) | ₹3k–15k/mo, all judgement outsourced | Black box; single-person key risk; liability stays with employer | Win on visibility; risk is the CA blocking (above) |
| Kredily / Zoho free tier | ₹0 up to a size gate | Filing layer paywalled (Kredily) / parity feature set (Zoho) | Win vs Kredily on filing; **parity vs Zoho** |
| A rival paid SaaS (Keka etc.) | ₹1k–2.5k/mo+ | Feature-led, not filing-guaranteed; opaque pricing | Win on filing SLA + price transparency (unverified rivals, §20 V-06) |

The distribution across these options is unknown and it is the *volume* variable behind the bureau pool (§04.3) and the "who is the incumbent" question (PRD §20, V-01–V-02). If most of the beachhead is on Tally-plus-CA, the wedge is displacement-with-migration; if most is on a rival SaaS, it is competitive win/loss. These are different GTM motions and the §20 studies decide which one we are running.

#### Worked example — one month in the life of a 60-person employer

To make the burden concrete rather than abstract, here is the recurring filing load for a single beachhead employer: a 60-person firm registered in Maharashtra and Karnataka (a common two-state footprint — HQ plus a satellite office). This is *one month*, and it repeats every month, forever.

| Date (typical) | Filing / action | Portal | Consequence of a miss |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7th | TDS deposit for prior month (u/s 192) | TRACES / bank challan | Interest 1.5%/month u/s 201; expense disallowance |
| 10th | Professional Tax return — Maharashtra (monthly if PTRC liability ≥ ₹1L/yr) | mahagst.gov.in | Penalty + interest per MSTPT Act |
| 15th | **EPF ECR** upload + challan for 60 employees | unifiedportal (EPFO) | 7Q interest 12% + 14B damages 5–25% |
| 15th | ESI contribution for eligible employees (< wage ceiling) | esic.gov.in | Damages up to 25% p.a.; benefit-denial liability |
| 20th | Professional Tax — Karnataka (monthly) | Karnataka commercial tax portal | Penalty per KTPTC&E Act |
| 21st | Shops & Establishment / labour welfare touchpoints | state labour portal | Registration lapse exposure |
| Month-end | Attendance close: OT reconciliation vs. 144-hr/quarter ceiling; leave accrual; wage-base recompute (two bases per the 50% add-back) | internal → payroll | Wrong PF/gratuity base → retro liability |
| Quarterly (Q-end +31d) | **Form 138** (ex-24Q) TDS return | TRACES | ₹200/day u/s 234E + penalty u/s 271H |
| Half-yearly | ESI return | esic.gov.in | Compliance flag |
| Annual | Form 130 (ex-Form 16); PF Form 3A/6A; PT annual (state); LWF (state) | multiple | Certificate/return defaults |

That is **six-plus distinct portals, three-plus statutory authorities, and at least four different filing cadences** for one 60-person firm in two states. Add a third state and the PT/LWF matrix multiplies again. This is the burden the product converts from a monthly scramble into a dated, tracked, executed pipeline — and it is why the *filing*, not the payslip, is the unit of delivery.

##### The cost of one missed month, in rupees

To size the *downside the product removes*, run the penalty math on a single missed EPF month for this 60-person firm. Assume total monthly PF remittance (employee + employer) of ₹1.2 lakh (60 employees, blended ₹2,000/head).

- **7Q interest:** 12% p.a. simple on ₹1.2 lakh for, say, a 3-month delay ≈ ₹1.2L × 12% × 3/12 = **₹3,600**.
- **14B damages:** delay-slab-based, 5% p.a. for up to 2 months' delay rising to 25% p.a. beyond 6 months. At a mid-slab 10% p.a. for 3 months ≈ ₹1.2L × 10% × 3/12 = **₹3,000**. [Verified — slab structure; exact slab boundaries to reconfirm against EPF Scheme para 32A.]
- **The uninsurable part:** the employer, not the bureau, receives the 7Q/14B order, and repeated default risks prosecution under the Code. The reputational and audit cost dwarfs the ~₹6,600 arithmetic.

The point is not the exact rupee figure — it is that a *single portal missed by one person on leave* costs more than a month of the product, every time, and the buyer has no forewarning today. Filing-status visibility is not a nicety; it is the insurance the retainer was supposed to buy and does not.

#### The state-fragmentation multiplier

Professional Tax and Labour Welfare Fund are **state subjects** — there is no single national schema. Every state an employer operates in adds an independent levy with its own slab table, gender variants, periodicity, registration and filing cadence.

- **PT is levied by ~20+ states** (Maharashtra, Karnataka, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Kerala, etc.) and **absent in others** (e.g., Delhi, Haryana, UP, Rajasthan have no PT). A multi-state employer must track "levy yes/no" per state before even reaching slabs. [Verified as structural; per-state slabs [Hypothesis]]
- **LWF exists in ~14 states** with contribution amounts, employer/employee split and periodicity that differ by state and are revised on their own schedules. Frappe HR already ships PT across 15+ states and LWF across 14 free (PRD §5) — so multi-state PT/LWF is *not* a differentiator, it is table stakes to even enter.
- The maintenance consequence (PRD §13): a verified, gazette-sourced PT+LWF dataset for every state — levy, slabs, gender variants, periodicity, effective dates — is a **build dependency**, and only Telangana was verified across both research rounds. Aggregator PT tables are "materially disputed" and at least one widely-cited 2026 table reproduces a superseded structure (PRD §20, V-09). Building on unverified aggregator PT data is a correctness risk, not a shortcut.

To make the fragmentation concrete — and to show exactly why we must treat aggregator tables as suspect — here is the *shape* of the divergence across four common states. **Every rupee slab below is [Hypothesis] pending a gazette re-check per PRD §13/§20**; the structural facts (that these states levy PT, that they differ on periodicity and gender treatment) are [Verified as structural].

| State | PT ceiling / typical top slab | Periodicity | Notable divergence | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Maharashtra | ~₹200/mo (₹300 in the February slab to hit the ₹2,500 annual cap) | Monthly (PTRC) if liability ≥ ₹1L/yr, else annual | The "February top-up" month is a recurring engine bug source | Slabs [Hypothesis]; MSTPT Act structural [Verified] |
| Karnataka | ~₹200/mo above a ~₹25,000/mo wage threshold (revised 2023) | Monthly | Threshold revised recently — pre-2023 tables are wrong | Slabs [Hypothesis] |
| West Bengal | Graduated slabs to a ₹2,500/yr cap | Monthly/annual | Distinct slab boundaries from MH/KA | Slabs [Hypothesis] |
| Telangana | Graduated slabs to ₹2,500/yr cap | Monthly | **The only state verified across both research rounds** | [Verified, PRD §13] |

- LWF divergence is worse because it is smaller and less documented: contribution amounts of a few rupees to a few tens of rupees, split employer/employee at ratios that differ by state, remitted monthly/half-yearly/annually depending on the state. The absolute rupees are trivial; the *count of distinct rules to keep current* is the cost.

> [Hypothesis] The state-fragmentation load is a *moat if maintained, a liability if not*. It is precisely the work an open-source project (Frappe) cannot contractually guarantee to keep current — which is where the "maintained statutory SLA" positioning earns its price.
> **Kill criterion:** if a rival ships a *contractually guaranteed*, all-state PT/LWF update SLA before we do, the maintenance moat narrows to filing execution alone.

### 04.2 The denominator problem, and the one number that survives audit

Almost every published figure for "India HR tech market size" is unusable, and the PRD already killed the worst offenders. This section states the rule, then builds up from a government denominator.

#### Numbers that are banned as denominators

| Banned denominator | Size implied | Why it is wrong | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| "$23.32bn → $38.36bn India HR tech" | ~₹2,20,000 Cr → ₹3,60,000 Cr | Almost certainly a *global* figure mislabelled as India; no attribution | [Killed] (PRD §2) |
| 6.33 crore / 5.31 crore Udyam MSMEs | ~6 crore "employers" | Udyam registrations are not employers with payroll obligations; inflates by two orders of magnitude | [Killed] (PRD §2, §20) |
| 24,18,266 EPFO *registered* establishments | ~24 lakh | Registered ≠ contributing; two-thirds of PF codes are dormant | [Killed as denominator] (PRD §2) |

The pattern is consistent: every inflated number counts *entities that could theoretically owe payroll* rather than *entities that demonstrably run payroll now*. The correction is to use the one figure that reflects revealed obligation. This is not pedantry — a plan denominated on 5.31 crore and one denominated on 7.66 lakh differ by ~69×, and every downstream metric (share, penetration, CAC payback against TAM) inherits that error.

#### The audit-proof denominator: EPFO contributing establishments

| Metric | Value | Source | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EPFO **contributing** establishments (FY2023-24) | **7,66,254** | EPFO Annual Report, as on 31.03.2024 | [Verified] |
| EPFO registered establishments (same date) | 24,18,266 | EPFO | [Verified] |
| Ratio registered : contributing | **3.16×** | Derived | [Verified] |
| Contributing members (active UANs) | 7.37 Cr | EPFO | [Verified] |
| Mean contributing employees per contributing establishment | 96.2 | Derived (7.37 Cr ÷ 7.66 lakh) | [Verified, but see caution] |
| Contributing establishments with **>200** employees | 41,881 | EPFO Appendix-2(v) | [Verified] |
| *Registered* establishments with >200 accounts | 173,250 | EPFO Appendix-2(v) | [Verified] |

> Caution on the mean. 96.2 is a **right-skewed average**, not a typical establishment. A small number of very large contributing establishments (the 41,881 above 200 employees, and the tail above 2,000) pull the mean far above the median. The *typical* contributing establishment is much smaller than 96 people. Any per-establishment revenue model built on 96.2 as a "typical" seat count will overstate ARPU. Use the mean only for aggregate ceilings, never for per-account modelling.

**Standing denominator rule for this PRD:** every market size, share claim and funnel stage is denominated on **7,66,254 contributing establishments**, or a sub-band of it. Any figure denominated on registered establishments (24.18 lakh) or Udyam (5.31 crore) is retracted on sight.

One caveat the denominator itself carries, stated so it is not discovered later: EPFO contributing establishments **exclude** genuinely tiny employers below the EPF threshold that nonetheless owe TDS/ESI/PT, and exclude establishments exempted from EPF that run their own trusts. The denominator therefore slightly *understates* the count of entities with *some* statutory payroll obligation while being the honest ceiling for entities with the *full* obligation stack the product serves. We accept the understatement because it errs conservative — the opposite direction from every banned number.

##### Stress-test — what if the denominator itself moves?

The whole model rests on one [Verified] number (7,66,254). Discipline requires asking what happens if it is stale or mis-stated, because a data room will.

- **It is a point-in-time count (31.03.2024).** The contributing base grows with formalisation and net EPFO additions; by launch it may be ~5–10% higher. That moves SAM *up*, not down — so anchoring on the FY2023-24 figure is again the conservative choice. The kill risk is the reverse: a recession or mass EPF-exemption shift shrinking the contributing base, which would show up in the next EPFO Annual Report.
- **The exclusions are directional, not random.** Sub-20 TDS/ESI/PT-only employers (excluded) are precisely the <20 funnel band we serve free anyway (PRD §1); their absence from the denominator does not distort the *paid* beachhead. Exempted-trust establishments (excluded) skew large and enterprise — outside the beachhead. Both exclusions therefore fall mostly *outside* the 20–200 band, so the denominator is *more* accurate for the beachhead than for the whole market.
- **The refresh discipline:** re-pull the contributing count from each new EPFO Annual Report and restate every downstream figure; never let a 31.03.2024 number age silently into a 2027 deck. (Source: EPFO Annual Report series [Verified — cadence].)

> [Hypothesis] 7,66,254 is a stable-to-growing floor for the addressable base over the plan horizon.
> **Kill criterion:** if the next EPFO Annual Report shows the contributing base *falling* year-on-year, treat the market as contracting and re-test the entry thesis, not just the SAM arithmetic.

#### The share-ceiling calibration

greytHR — a market leader with a genuinely broad SMB base — claims ~**34,000 customers**, which is **4.4%** of the 7.66 lakh contributing establishments [Verified, PRD §2]. This is the single most useful number for sanity-checking any SOM: *that is what leadership looks like on the honest denominator.* Any three-year plan that implies more than low-single-digit percentage penetration of contributing establishments is claiming to out-penetrate the incumbent leader from a standing start, and should be rejected.

A second calibration sits alongside it: greytHR's realised **~₹52 PEPM** (filed revenue ÷ claimed platform scale, PRD §18). Read together, the two numbers say the *leader* of this market monetises ~4.4% of establishments at ~₹52/employee/month — and is not comfortably profitable (PRD §2). Any model that assumes both higher penetration *and* higher realised PEPM than the leader is asserting we out-execute the incumbent on both axes simultaneously, from zero. That is the specific claim the sensitivity grid in §04.3 is built to discipline.

#### The market funnel, stage by stage

The market-funnel diagram narrows from the inflated denominators the industry quotes to the number a founder can actually act on. Each step is a deliberate exclusion with a reason, not a haircut.

| Stage | Count | What it is | Why we narrow here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quoted "market" | 5.31 crore | Udyam MSME registrations | [Killed] — not employers with payroll obligations (PRD §2) |
| Registered universe | 24,18,266 | EPFO-registered establishments | [Killed as denominator] — 3.16× the contributing base; two-thirds dormant |
| **Addressable universe (TAM)** | **7,66,254** | EPFO *contributing* establishments | [Verified] — revealed payroll obligation; the honest ceiling |
| Serviceable (SAM) | ~1.8–2.6 lakh (+ tranche of 41,881 >200) | 20–200 beachhead + near-in expansion | Obligation + budget + dissatisfaction overlap; product shape fits |
| Winnable in 3 yrs (SOM) | ~1,100–3,900 establishments | 0.5–1.5% of a 2.2-lakh beachhead | Bounded by greytHR's 4.4% leadership ceiling and cold-start reality |

The funnel discipline is the section's core contribution: the difference between the top row (5.31 crore) and the SOM row (~2,200 establishments at the 1% midpoint) is **five orders of magnitude**, and almost every published India-HR-tech number lives in the top two rows. Building a plan on 7,66,254 and narrowing transparently is what makes the SAM defensible in a data room.

#### Demand-side evidence of dissatisfaction

"Dissatisfaction" is the softest leg of the obligation-budget-dissatisfaction stool, so it needs its own evidence rather than assertion.

- **Implementation friction is the most-cited churn trigger in the market** (PRD §16), and it concentrates at **mid-year cutover** — opening balances, YTD earnings, TDS already deducted, previous-employer income, investment declarations mid-cycle, certificate continuity across two systems, EPF UAN and ESI IP continuity, leave balances, gratuity accrual. The pain of *switching* is itself evidence that the installed base is unhappy but stuck. It also cuts the other way for us: the same friction is a moat *once we hold the record*, which is why migration is a P0 product surface, not a services task (PRD §16).
- **The incumbent's own limits create dissatisfaction.** Tally is statutorily complete but cannot file-as-a-service, offers no employee surface, no mobile app and no CA console (PRD §5). Kredily paywalls challans, Form 12BB and Form 16 — the *filing* layer sits behind the free calculation. The employer who "has software" still hits a wall at the exact moment of filing.
- **The bureau black box (Pain 3) is dissatisfaction by another name** — no filing-status visibility, single-person key risk, and the employer carrying liability for the CA's errors.

> [Hypothesis] Dissatisfaction is real but its *magnitude and willingness-to-switch* are unmeasured — no NPS, churn-rate or win/loss data exists in the corpus.
> **Kill criterion:** buyer interviews (PRD §20, V-01–V-03, V-05). If beachhead employers report high satisfaction with the Tally-plus-CA status quo and low switching intent, the wedge is weaker than the burden analysis implies, and acquisition CAC assumptions must rise.

##### Acceptance criteria — the denominator discipline

- **AC-10 (single denominator).** Every share, penetration and SAM figure in any downstream deck resolves to 7,66,254 (or a named sub-band); a reviewer can trace it in one step. Any figure that cannot is retracted.
- **AC-11 (no skew laundering).** No per-account revenue figure multiplies by 96.2; the mean is used only for aggregate ceilings, flagged as such.
- **AC-12 (band resolution gate).** Before any funding model hardens, the 20–200 band count is resolved from EPFO Appendix-2, replacing the 1.8–2.6 lakh [Hypothesis] range (PRD §20, adjacent to V-06).

### 04.3 TAM / SAM / SOM on the honest denominator

We size the market two ways and reconcile them: **top-down by establishment count × realised ARPU**, and **bottom-up from filed vendor revenue**. Both must agree, or the model is wrong.

#### Establishment counts by band

The beachhead is 20–200. We know the two ends precisely (EPF turns on at 20; 41,881 contributing establishments sit above 200) but the *interior* band distribution needs the EPFO Appendix-2 size table pulled band-by-band.

| Band (contributing employees) | Contributing establishments | Basis | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total contributing (all sizes) | 7,66,254 | EPFO 31.03.2024 | [Verified] |
| > 200 (expansion + enterprise) | 41,881 | EPFO Appendix-2(v) | [Verified] |
| ≤ 200 (residual, all bands below) | ~7,24,373 | Derived (7,66,254 − 41,881) | [Verified as residual] |
| **20–200 (beachhead)** | **~1,80,000–2,60,000** | See note | **[Hypothesis]** |
| < 20 (funnel/acquisition only) | remainder of the ≤200 residual | See note | [Hypothesis] |

> Note on the beachhead count. The ≤200 residual (7.24 lakh) mixes genuine 20–200 employers with a large tail of small (<20) contributing establishments — voluntary coverage, seasonal, and near-dormant codes that still remit. Splitting the residual requires the band-level EPFO Appendix-2 table (10–20, 20–50, 50–100, 100–200). Pending that, the beachhead is modelled at **~1.8–2.6 lakh contributing establishments** — a deliberately wide range.
> **Kill criterion:** pull EPFO Appendix-2 band distribution (a desk task, no field work — adjacent to PRD §20, V-06). If the 20–200 band resolves below ~1.5 lakh contributing establishments, SAM shrinks and the "expansion into 200–2,000" phase must be pulled forward.

A sanity check on why the range is centred near 2.2 lakh rather than higher: if contributing establishments were distributed like the mean (96.2) suggested, most of the 7.24 lakh residual would sit in the 20–200 band. But the mean is right-skewed (§04.2), which means the *median* establishment is well below 96 and a large share of the residual is likely <20 — voluntary/near-dormant codes. That pushes the honest beachhead count *below* a naive "most of 7.24 lakh" read, which is why 1.8–2.6 lakh, not 4–5 lakh, is the modelled range. Resolving this is AC-12 above.

**A back-of-envelope reconstruction, stated so its assumptions can be attacked.** Employment in India follows a steep power law; the standard read is that a large majority of contributing establishments are small (voluntary coverage, <20 heads) while a thin tail carries most of the members. Take the two verified anchors — 7,66,254 total contributing establishments, 41,881 above 200 — and layer a plausible size split on the 7,24,373 that sit at ≤200:

| ≤200 sub-band | Illustrative share of the ≤200 residual | Establishments | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| < 20 (funnel only) | ~65% | ~4.71 lakh | Right-skew: most contributing codes are small/voluntary |
| 20–50 | ~22% | ~1.59 lakh | The populous lower beachhead |
| 50–100 | ~8% | ~0.58 lakh | 50–200 "carry revenue" (PRD §1) |
| 100–200 | ~5% | ~0.36 lakh | Thinning toward the >200 tail |
| **20–200 total (beachhead)** | ~35% | **~2.53 lakh** | Sum of the three middle bands |

Flex the <20 share to ~75% (heavier small-code skew) and the beachhead falls to ~1.81 lakh; flex it to ~55% and it rises to ~3.26 lakh. That is precisely the ~1.8–2.6 lakh modelled range (the 3.26-lakh upper flex is deliberately excluded as optimistic), and it exposes the one number that moves everything: **the <20 share of the residual**. The illustrative shares above are **[Hypothesis]** — no band-level source underpins them; they are a shape, not a measurement.
> **Kill criterion (restates AC-12):** the EPFO Appendix-2 band table (10–20 / 20–50 / 50–100 / 100–200) is a desk pull, not field work. If it lands the 20–200 band below ~1.5 lakh, SAM shrinks by up to a third and the 200–2,000 expansion phase must be pulled forward; if above ~2.6 lakh, the beachhead is larger than modelled and the SOM grids in §04.3 are conservative. Either way, no funding model hardens on the reconstruction — only on the pulled table.

#### Top-down market model

We use **realised** PEPM, not list price. The only two realised anchors that survived audit are **₹52 PEPM** (greytHR, SMB-weighted) and **₹126 PEPM** (PeopleStrong, enterprise-weighted), both derived from filed revenue over claimed platform scale and both biased *downward* because platform users exceed billed seats (PRD §18). For the beachhead we anchor on **₹80–150 PEPM** as a [Hypothesis] band — above the greytHR realised floor (because our thesis is that filing-as-a-service commands more than commodity SMB HR) and below the enterprise anchor (because we do not sell enterprise features).

Per-account revenue requires a *billable* seat count, not the skewed mean. We model the beachhead average billable headcount at **~55 employees** (the segment centre of mass — 50–200 "carry revenue" per PRD §1, blended with the 20–50 tail).

| Layer | Definition | Establishments | Avg billable seats | PEPM | Annual value | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **TAM** | All contributing establishments as a software-addressable universe | 7,66,254 | 96.2 (mean, aggregate only) | ₹80–150 | see reconciliation below | [Hypothesis] |
| **SAM** | Beachhead 20–200 + near-in expansion 200–2,000 | ~1.8–2.6 lakh (20–200) + tranche of 41,881 (>200) | ~55 (beachhead) | ₹80–150 | **₹950 Cr – ₹2,570 Cr** | [Hypothesis] |
| **SOM (3-yr)** | Realistic capture at sub-leadership share | 0.5–1.5% of beachhead | ~55 | ₹80–150 | **₹5 Cr – ₹32 Cr ARR** | [Hypothesis] |

SAM worked example (beachhead only, midpoints): 2.2 lakh establishments × 55 seats × ₹115 PEPM × 12 = **₹1,670 Cr/yr** addressable in the 20–200 band alone. Adding a serviceable slice of the 200–2,000 expansion band lifts SAM toward ₹2,000–2,600 Cr.

SOM worked example (3-yr): at **1.0%** of a 2.2-lakh beachhead = 2,200 paying establishments × 55 seats × ₹115 × 12 = **₹16.7 Cr ARR**. The 4.4% greytHR ceiling implies an absolute upper bound near ₹73 Cr ARR on the beachhead — reachable only at multi-year leadership, not in three years from zero.

#### Bottom-up reconciliation (the reality check)

The top-down SAM must reconcile with money actually being spent. It does:

- **Filed revenue across 11 Indian HRMS entities: ₹1,374 Cr.** Grossed up for unfiled and foreign vendors → **₹2,100–3,900 Cr** real annual India HRMS software spend (USD 0.24–0.45bn at ₹94.43/USD) [Verified, PRD §2].
- Our SAM midpoint (~₹1,670 Cr, beachhead only) is **~43–80% of total current software spend** — which is exactly right, because the beachhead is the largest single band and current spend also includes sub-20 and enterprise. The model is internally consistent.
- **Corrected CAGR ceiling: ₹10,905 Cr at 10% CAGR** (not ₹12,250 Cr — that figure was overstated 12.3% and is [Killed], PRD §2). This is the *whole-market* growth ceiling, not a target.

The reconciliation is the single most important integrity check in this section. A top-down SAM that *exceeded* total observed software spend would be self-refuting (you cannot address more than the market spends). A top-down SAM that landed at, say, 5% of observed spend would mean we had mis-defined the beachhead as a niche. Landing at ~43–80% of current spend — with the balance explained by sub-20 free tiers and enterprise suites we deliberately decline — is the outcome that says the two independent methods describe the same market.

#### SAM/SOM sensitivity — the model is a range, so show the range

Because both the beachhead establishment count and realised PEPM are unvalidated, the responsible presentation is a grid, not a headline. SOM ARR = (beachhead establishments) × (share) × (avg billable seats, held at 55) × (PEPM) × 12.

**Beachhead SAM (₹ Cr/yr) at full penetration — establishment count × PEPM (55 seats):**

| Establishments ↓ / PEPM → | ₹80 | ₹115 | ₹150 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.8 lakh | ₹950 Cr | ₹1,366 Cr | ₹1,782 Cr |
| 2.2 lakh | ₹1,162 Cr | ₹1,670 Cr | ₹2,178 Cr |
| 2.6 lakh | ₹1,373 Cr | ₹1,974 Cr | ₹2,574 Cr |

**3-year SOM (₹ Cr ARR) at 2.2-lakh beachhead — share × PEPM (55 seats):**

| Share ↓ / PEPM → | ₹80 | ₹115 | ₹150 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.5% | ₹5.8 Cr | ₹8.3 Cr | ₹10.9 Cr |
| 1.0% | ₹11.6 Cr | ₹16.7 Cr | ₹21.8 Cr |
| 1.5% | ₹17.4 Cr | ₹25.0 Cr | ₹32.7 Cr |

Reading the grids: even the optimistic corner of a 3-yr SOM (1.5% share, ₹150 PEPM) is **₹32.7 Cr ARR** — a third of the greytHR-ceiling upper bound (~₹73 Cr) and comfortably inside "credible for a well-executed new entrant." The pessimistic corner (0.5% share, ₹80 PEPM) is **₹5.8 Cr ARR** — survivable but thin. The spread between corners is ~5.6×, which is *entirely* driven by the two unvalidated inputs (share and PEPM). That is the quantified reason the §20 validation programme gates funding: the model's uncertainty is not noise, it is two specific studies wide.

A third variable — average billable seats, held at 55 throughout — is worth a sensitivity note even though we do not grid it. If the realised beachhead average is 40 (heavier 20–50 weighting) rather than 55, every ARR figure above scales by 40/55 ≈ 0.73×; the 1.0%/₹115 midpoint drops from ₹16.7 Cr to ~₹12.1 Cr. If it is 70 (heavier 100–200 weighting), the midpoint rises to ~₹21.2 Cr. Seat count is a *third* study (won-deal seat sizes, PRD §20, V-03) that the grid holds constant only for legibility.

> Why TAM is expressed as a range, not a point. Multiplying 7.66 lakh × 96.2 × ₹115 × 12 yields a nonsense ~₹10,000 Cr "TAM" that (a) uses the skewed mean as a per-account seat count and (b) assumes 100% software penetration at full PEPM. That number is arithmetically adjacent to the ₹10,905 Cr *CAGR ceiling* and would be easy to launder into a deck. **Do not.** The honest TAM statement is: *current revealed spend ₹2,100–3,900 Cr, whole-market 10% ceiling ₹10,905 Cr, beachhead SAM ~₹1.7–2.6k Cr.*
