## 06. The Statutory Compliance Spine

This section is the consolidated statutory register the rest of the product is
built around. §01 of Draft 1 established the thesis — **the statutory filing, not
the payslip, is the unit of delivery** — and that the customer's problem changes
at headcount thresholds, so the feature gates should mirror the obligation gates
exactly. This section makes that concrete: every statute the payroll engine must
compute, who it binds, at what threshold, on what cadence, with what penalty for
failure, the data it consumes, and the product requirement it generates.

A note on how to read this. The engine is **rules-first, LLM-last** (§08, Verified):
no statutory or monetary figure is ever model-generated. Everything in this section
is therefore a specification for a deterministic rule, versioned and effective-dated,
not a prompt. Where a claim carries a confidence marker, it is because the underlying
notification was either verified against gazette/primary source, is inferred and
needs validation, or was believed and disproven. The standing rule from §02 holds
without exception: **no compliance claim ships without a gazette, notified-rule or
regulator citation captured with URL and date, and "check for a corrigendum" is a
non-negotiable step** — the November 2026 EPF analysis inverted twice across two
research rounds precisely because a corrigendum was missed.

Scope note (phasing). Consistent with the beachhead decision (§05, 20–200 employees),
the P0 filings in this spine are **ECR, ESI challan, PT return, Form 138 and
Form 130** for single-state and early multi-state tenants. Bonus (§06.7),
compulsory gratuity insurance (§06.6) and the enterprise-scale registers under the
Codes are correct-by-construction in the data model from v1 but their filing
surfaces phase in with the mid-market expansion (§05). This section specifies the
whole spine; it does not imply the whole spine ships in one release.



**Figure 36. Statutory Step Function**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    classDef step fill:#0b3d2e,stroke:#0f5c46,color:#eafff5,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef gate fill:#1d1a3a,stroke:#3b357a,color:#ecebff,stroke-width:1px;
    classDef spine fill:#5a1e1e,stroke:#8f2f2f,color:#ffecec,stroke-width:1px;

    S0["HC 1-9<br/>TDS on salary (24Q)<br/>from Rupee 1"]:::step
    S10["HC 10+<br/>+ Professional Tax (state)<br/>+ Shops/Estab & LWF"]:::step
    S20["HC 20+<br/>+ EPF/EPS (EPFO)<br/>ECR monthly"]:::step
    SBIG["HC 50-200<br/>revenue-carrying band<br/>full statutory stack"]:::step

    ESI{{"ESI: 10+ or 20+<br/>threshold varies by state"}}:::gate
    GRAT{{"Gratuity: any HC<br/>triggers at 5-yr tenure<br/>(time-based, not HC)"}}:::gate

    SPINE["Filing calendar = product spine<br/>each step adds a recurring return"]:::spine

    S0 --> S10 --> S20 --> SBIG
    S10 -.state rule.-> ESI
    S20 -.state rule.-> ESI
    ESI -.-> SBIG
    GRAT -.overlays all bands.-> SPINE
    S0 --> SPINE
    S10 --> SPINE
    S20 --> SPINE
    SBIG --> SPINE
```


### 06.1 The obligation step function — what turns on, and when

Indian labour and social-security law is a step function on headcount. The
obligation is absent below a threshold and mandatory at or above it, and the test
for "at or above" is not always "today's count" — several thresholds latch on a
look-back window, so the obligation, once triggered, does not switch off when the
count dips. This latching behaviour is a first-class data-model requirement, not
an edge case.

| Headcount | Obligation that turns on | Look-back / latch rule | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** (no threshold) | TDS u/s 192 (monthly deposit, quarterly return, annual certificate); Shops & Establishments registration; minimum wages / floor wage; prescribed-format appointment letter | Applies from the first employee, permanently | Income-tax Act s.192; state S&E Acts; Code on Wages 2019 s.5–9 **[Verified]** |
| **10** | ESI; gratuity accrual; maternity benefit; wage/attendance registers in prescribed electronic form | ESI/gratuity test reads "employed on any day of the preceding twelve months" — **latches once crossed** | ESI Act 1948 s.1(3); Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 s.1(3); Maternity Benefit Act 1961 **[Verified]** |
| **20** | **EPF** (and EPS/EDLI); **Payment of Bonus** (s.1(3)(b)); grievance redressal committee | "20 or more persons employed on any day of the preceding year"; **both EPF and Bonus latch** | EPF & MP Act 1952 s.1(3)(b); Payment of Bonus Act 1965 s.1(3)(b); Code on Social Security 2020 s.1(4) **[Verified]** |
| **50** | Crèche facility | Notified Rules under OSH Code | OSH&WC Code 2020; Central Rules notified 8 May 2026 **[Verified]** |
| **100** | Works committee | Threshold under Industrial Relations Code | IR Code 2020 s.3 **[Verified]** |
| **300** | Government approval for retrenchment, lay-off and closure; standing orders | **Raised from 100** by the new Codes | IR Code 2020 s.77 / Chapter X **[Verified]** |

Three corrections carried forward from Draft 1, so they are not re-introduced:

- **Sub-20 companies are not obligation-free.** TDS, S&E, minimum wages and the
  prescribed appointment letter all bind from employee one. A payroll product for
  a 12-person firm has real statutory work to do; only EPF and Bonus are genuinely
  absent below 20. **[Killed]** (the "no obligation below 20" framing)
- **Employee's Compensation is not a blanket sub-10 liability.** The Second Schedule
  limits it to largely hazardous and mechanical occupations; do not model it as a
  universal small-employer cost. **[Killed]**
- **The 40+ periodic health check-up** is confined by the notified Rules to docks,
  mines and construction, in permissive language — not a general obligation. **[Killed]**

**Who counts toward the threshold — the head-counting rule is itself statutory.**
The count is not "employees on the payroll today." Edge cases the derivation must
encode:

- **Contract labour counts** toward EPF/ESI coverage of the principal employer
  where the contractor is not independently covered; the principal employer carries
  residual liability for contractor employees' PF/ESI. (Source: EPF Act s.8A; ESI
  Act s.40; CoSS s.30) **[Verified]**
- **Apprentices engaged under the Apprentices Act 1961 are excluded** from EPF, ESI,
  gratuity and bonus counts; NEEM/NAPS trainees are treated similarly. Company-
  designated "trainees" who are not statutory apprentices **do count**. (Source:
  Apprentices Act s.18; EPF Act s.2(f) exclusion) **[Verified]**
- **Directors** who draw salary and are not merely equity holders count as employees
  for ESI/PF where an employer-employee relationship exists; a non-executive director
  paid only sitting fees does not. **[Hypothesis]** — the ESIC position on directors
  has shifted; **kill criterion: confirm director inclusion against the current ESIC
  circular and the establishment's actual engagement terms before enrolling.**
- **Part-time, casual, seasonal and daily-rated workers** count toward the ESI/EPF
  headcount test on the "employed on any day" reading, even if not working today.

**Product implication.** The tenant's obligation profile is derived, never
declared. The engine computes it from (headcount time-series × establishment
type × state × sector × engagement-type mix), re-derives it every payroll period,
and **latches** any obligation whose look-back window has been crossed. When a
tenant crosses 20 for the first time, EPF enrolment, UAN generation, ECR filing and
bonus eligibility must appear as tasks automatically — the customer should not have
to know the threshold exists. This is the direct product expression of "the feature
gates mirror the obligation gates exactly" (§01). The latch also means an obligation
must be **explicitly retired**, never silently dropped when headcount falls: the
engine records the trigger event, the look-back window, and the (rare) statutory
exit condition, so an auditor can see why an obligation is still active at 17 heads.

---

### 06.2 EPF — Employees' Provident Fund

**What it is.** A defined-contribution retirement scheme with three sub-schemes
riding on the same base wage: the Provident Fund (EPF), the pension (EPS 1995),
and the linked insurance (EDLI 1976). It is the single most consequential
statutory computation in Indian payroll and, per §01, the reason the beachhead
begins at 20 employees.

**Who it binds.** Every establishment employing **20 or more** persons, on any
day of the preceding year (latches). Voluntary coverage is possible below 20 by
agreement (s.1(4)). An employee earning **above ₹15,000/month basic + DA at the
time of joining** may be treated as an "excluded employee" (not compulsorily
enrolled if never previously a member); once a member, they remain a member even if
wages later exceed the ceiling. (Source: EPF Scheme para 2(f), para 26A) **[Verified]**

**Thresholds and rates.**

| Item | Value | Note | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Statutory wage ceiling | **₹15,000/month** | PF is computed on min(PF wages, 15,000) unless the employer opts for actual wages | EPF Scheme para 26A; EPS para 3 **[Verified]** |
| Employee contribution | **12%** of PF wages | Re-notified under Scheme 2026 by **S.O. 3582(E)**, retrospective to 21.11.2025 | EPFO S.O. 3582(E) **[Verified]** |
| Employer contribution | **12%**, split: **8.33% to EPS** (capped at 8.33% of ₹15,000 = ₹1,250) + **3.67% to EPF** | The EPS split and the ₹1,250 cap are the classic source of computation error | EPS para 3(1) proviso **[Verified]** |
| Reduced rate (10%) | 10% for ≤19 employees, sick units, and specified sectors (jute, beedi, brick, coir, guar gum) | A notified variable — must be effective-dated per establishment class, not assumed 12% | EPF Scheme para 26B / notified list **[Verified]** |
| EDLI | **0.50%** of PF wages (max wage ₹15,000) | Employer-only | EDLI Scheme para 8A **[Verified]** |
| EPF admin charges | **0.50%** of PF wages, min ₹500/month (₹75 if no contributory member) | Employer-only, revised w.e.f. 01.06.2018 | EPFO notification, 2018 **[Verified]** |
| EDLI admin charges | Nil (waived) | Waived since 01.04.2017 | EPFO circular **[Verified]** |

Worked example (one employee, PF wages ₹15,000, employer contributes on ceiling):

| Head | Rate | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Employee EPF | 12% | ₹1,800 |
| Employer EPS | 8.33% (capped) | ₹1,250 |
| Employer EPF | balance of 12% | ₹550 |
| EDLI | 0.50% | ₹75 |
| EPF admin | 0.50% | ₹75 |
| **Total remitted per employee** | | **₹3,750** |



**Figure 37. Eps Three Way Split**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["Employer statutory cost per member (worked example, PF wage ₹15,000)"]
    START --> C12["Provident-fund 12% share = ₹1,800"]
    START --> EDLI["EDLI 0.50% = ₹75 (employer only)"]
    START --> ADMIN["EPF admin 0.50%, min ₹500 = ₹75 (employer only)"]

    C12 --> Q1{"Is the member an EPS member?"}
    Q1 -->|"First joined on/after 01.09.2014 with PF wage over ₹15,000"| NOEPS["EPS = ₹0 - full 12% goes to EPF"]
    Q1 -->|"Eligible EPS member"| Q2{"Employer PF election"}

    Q2 -->|"On ceiling: base = min of wage and ₹15,000"| CEIL["EPS = 8.33% x 15,000 = ₹1,250 (capped)<br/>EPF = ₹1,800 - ₹1,250 = ₹550"]
    Q2 -->|"On actual wage over ₹15,000"| ACT["EPS 8.33% but STILL CAPPED at ₹1,250<br/>EPF = 12% of actual wage - ₹1,250<br/>all excess lands in EPF, never EPS"]

    NOEPS --> EPFACC[["EPF account (member PF)"]]
    CEIL --> EPFACC
    ACT --> EPFACC
    CEIL --> EPSACC[["EPS 1995 pension (hard cap ₹1,250)"]]
    ACT --> EPSACC

    EPFACC --> NOTE["Split is driven by TWO independent elections, not one:<br/>1) ceiling vs actual wage  2) EPS-cap at ₹1,250<br/>Worked total remitted per employee = ₹3,750<br/>EE 12% ₹1,800 + ER EPS ₹1,250 + ER EPF ₹550 + EDLI ₹75 + admin ₹75"]
    EPSACC --> NOTE
    EDLI --> NOTE
    ADMIN --> NOTE
```


Note the employer's ₹1,800 splits **₹1,250 to EPS + ₹550 to EPF**, not 8.33%/3.67%
of actual wages, because EPS is capped at ₹1,250. A payroll engine that applies
8.33% to actual wages above the ceiling mis-allocates the pension share — one of
the most common bugs in Indian payroll software, and a legally material one because
it changes the employee's pension entitlement. A second, subtler bug: when the
employer opts for **actual-wage** PF above ₹15,000, EPS *still* caps at ₹1,250, so
the entire excess (12% of the amount above ₹15,000 plus the 3.67% share) lands in
**EPF**, not EPS. The three-way split is a function of two independent elections
(ceiling-vs-actual, and EPS-cap), not one.

**EPS eligibility and higher-pension edge cases.**

- **EPS membership closes to new high earners.** An employee who **first joins EPF
  on or after 01.09.2014 with PF wages above ₹15,000** is *not* an EPS member — the
  full 12% employer share goes to EPF, EPS is zero. The engine must branch on
  first-join date and first-join wage, not on current wage. (Source: EPS para 6A,
  as amended 22.08.2014) **[Verified]**
- **Higher pension on actual wages.** The Supreme Court (04.11.2022, *EPFO v Sunil
  Kumar*) upheld the amended EPS permitting eligible members to contribute EPS on
  actual wages above ₹15,000, with EPFO opening and repeatedly extending an
  application window. A tenant with opted-in employees needs EPS computed on actual
  wages for exactly those members. **[Hypothesis]** — the operational rules,
  arrears-recovery mechanics and the final application deadline have shifted several
  times; **kill criterion: confirm each opted member's EPFO higher-pension approval
  status and the prevailing EPFO circular before computing EPS above the ceiling —
  do not infer it from wage level.**
- **Pensionable age 58**, minimum 10 years' eligible service; early (reduced) pension
  from 50. These gate EPS *claims* (Forms 10C/10D), not monthly ECR, but the
  service ledger must support them. (Source: EPS paras 12, 12A) **[Verified]**

**VPF and taxability of high contributions.** Voluntary Provident Fund (VPF) lets an
employee contribute **above 12%** with no matching employer obligation; it rides the
same account. But interest on employee contributions (EPF+VPF) **exceeding ₹2.5
lakh/year** is taxable (₹5 lakh where there is no employer contribution). (Source:
Finance Act 2021, provisos to s.10(11)/(12); Rule 9D) **[Verified]** The engine must
track cumulative annual employee contribution to flag the taxable-interest threshold —
a Form 16 / Form 130 input, not just a payroll line.

**The wage-splitting precedent.** Before the Codes, the Supreme Court (28.02.2019,
*RPFC v Vivekananda Vidyamandir*) held that allowances **ordinarily, uniformly and
necessarily paid to all** employees are "basic wages" for PF — employers cannot
carve the PF base down by relabelling universal pay as "special allowance." This is
the case-law ancestor of the Codes' 50% add-back (§06.10) and still governs pre-Code
periods that a retro run might touch. (Source: SC Civil Appeal 6221/2011) **[Verified]**

**Arrears, LOP and mid-month join/exit.** PF is computed on wages **actually earned**
in the month: loss-of-pay days reduce PF wages proportionately; salary arrears
attract PF **for the month(s) to which they relate**, not the month paid (this is a
retro-recompute, §06.10). A mid-month joiner accrues PF on the part-month wage. The
₹15,000 ceiling is **not** pro-rated for a part month unless the employer's rule
pro-rates the ceiling — a per-tenant policy the engine must hold. **[Verified]**

**International Workers (IW).** An IW (a foreign national working in India for a
covered establishment, or an Indian working abroad in an SSA country) contributes on
**full wages with no ₹15,000 ceiling**, unless exempt under a Social Security
Agreement via a Certificate of Coverage. India has SSAs with ~20 countries. (Source:
EPF Scheme para 83; EPS para 43A) **[Hypothesis]** — the Karnataka High Court
(*Stone Hill Education Foundation*, 2024) struck down the IW special provisions as
unconstitutional and the matter is under challenge; **kill criterion: confirm the
current enforceability of para 83 (and any SC stay/ruling) before applying uncapped
IW contributions — this is a live, contested rule.**

**UAN, Aadhaar seeding and the Joint Declaration — the operational chokepoint.**
The UAN (Universal Account Number) is the member's permanent PF identity across
employers. An ECR is accepted only for members whose UAN is **Aadhaar-seeded and
KYC-verified**; an un-seeded or name/DOB-mismatched UAN fails silently at upload, so
the member's contribution is not credited even though the challan clears. Where a
member's name, date of birth, father's name, date of joining or date of exit is
wrong in EPFO records, the correction now runs through the **Joint Declaration (JD)**
— an employer-attested online form, since the 2024 SOP tightened the process and
required documentary proof plus (for some fields) employer digital signature. A
pending JD blocks the member's claims (Form 19/10C/10D) and can block ECR credit.
The engine must therefore hold KYC/seeding **state per member**, surface a
mismatch-and-JD queue **before** the filing window, and never treat "UAN exists" as
"UAN filable." (Source: EPFO UAN/KYC SOP; Joint Declaration SOP circular, 2024)
**[Hypothesis]** — the JD field list and proof requirements were revised more than
once in 2024–25; **kill criterion: confirm the current JD-permissible fields and
proof matrix against the latest EPFO circular before building the correction flow.**

**Government employer-share subsidies (ABRY / PMRPY) are a contribution branch, not
a discount.** Under employment-incentive schemes the government pays part or all of
the *employer's* (and sometimes the *employee's*) share for eligible new joiners for
a fixed window — PMRPY paid the full 12%+12% for eligible members (registration
window now closed); ABRY (Aatmanirbhar Bharat Rozgar Yojana) subsidised new low-wage
hires. Where a member is enrolled under such a scheme, the ECR must still *report* the
full statutory contribution but the **employer's remittance is reduced by the
subsidised portion**, reconciled against the scheme's eligibility (wage ceiling, new-
vs-existing member, registration date). Modelling the subsidy as a flat rate cut
mis-states both the ECR and the remittance. (Source: EPFO ABRY/PMRPY scheme
guidelines) **[Hypothesis]** — these schemes have hard, expired or rolling
registration windows and any successor scheme (e.g. the 2024-announced ELI
employment-linked incentives) carries fresh eligibility rules; **kill criterion:
verify which scheme, if any, is open and the member's eligibility against the current
EPFO/MoLE scheme notification before applying a subsidised employer share — do not
carry a lapsed scheme forward.**

**Filing cadence.**

- **ECR (Electronic Challan-cum-Return)** — monthly, due by the **15th** of the
  following month. This is the master filing: it carries wages, contributions and
  member-level detail in one file, and the challan is generated from it.
- **Annual accounts** — EPFO now maintains member passbooks; the legacy Forms 3A/6A
  are effectively subsumed by the monthly ECR, but the engine must still be able to
  reproduce a 3A/6A-equivalent register for audit and for migration from Tally,
  which still emits them.
- **Onboarding/exit forms** — Form 11 (declaration on joining), Form 2 (nomination),
  Form 5/10 (new joiners / exits, now folded into ECR), Form 19/10C/10D (withdrawal/
  pension claims, employee-initiated via UAN).

**Penalties for late/non-payment.**

| Failure | Consequence | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Late deposit | Interest u/s 7Q at **12% p.a.** on the amount due | EPF Act s.7Q **[Verified]** |
| Delayed remittance (damages) | Damages u/s 14B, historically graded by delay: **<2 months 5%, 2–<4 months 10%, 4–<6 months 15%, 6+ months 25% p.a.** (para 32A) | EPF Act s.14B; para 32A **[Hypothesis]** — the graded 14B scale has been contested/rationalised in recent EPFO circulars and by tribunal rulings on mens rea; **kill criterion: verify the current 14B damages slab against the latest EPFO notification and any corrigendum before quoting a rate to a customer** |
| Non-enrolment of eligible employee | Recovery of arrears + interest + damages; prosecution u/s 14 | EPF Act s.14 **[Verified]** |

**Data required.** PF wages (per the wage-definition rule, §06.10), UAN, Aadhaar-
seeded and KYC-verified UAN status, date of joining/exit, first-join date and
first-join wage (for EPS eligibility branching), "excluded employee" flag and its
basis, IW status and Certificate-of-Coverage reference, higher-pension election and
EPFO approval status, VPF election, nomination, and the employer's ceiling-vs-actual
election. UAN KYC-seeding status gates ECR acceptance — an un-seeded UAN silently
fails, so the engine must surface seeding state before the filing window, not after
rejection.

**Product implication.** ECR generation and filing is a P0 artefact (§01 names ECR
first in the filings list). The engine must: (a) compute the three-way employer
split correctly against the EPS cap under **both** ceiling and actual elections;
(b) branch EPS on first-join date/wage and honour per-member higher-pension approvals;
(c) pre-validate UAN KYC state; (d) reproduce 3A/6A-equivalent registers for Tally
migration; (e) track cumulative employee contribution for the ₹2.5L taxable-interest
flag; (f) support the 10% reduced-rate establishment classes; and (g) build against
**Scheme 2026**, not the repealed 1952 Scheme (see §06.9). The 12% is a notified
variable, not a constant — effective-date it.

---

### 06.3 ESI — Employees' State Insurance

**What it is.** A contributory health-insurance and cash-benefit scheme
(medical, sickness, maternity, disablement, dependants' benefit) administered by
ESIC, funded by employer + employee contributions on gross wages.

**Who it binds.** Establishments (as notified, by area and class) employing
**10 or more** persons, covering employees earning **up to ₹21,000/month gross**
(₹25,000 for employees with disability). The ₹21,000 is a **coverage ceiling on
gross wages**, distinct from EPF's ₹15,000 ceiling — the two bases diverge on the
same payslip. Note ESI is **area-notified**: an establishment in a district ESIC
has not notified is not covered even at 10+ heads, so the engine's coverage test is
(headcount × area-notification × wage), not headcount alone. (Source: ESI Act
s.1(3); ESIC implementation notifications by district) **[Verified]**

**Thresholds and rates.**

| Item | Value | Note | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wage coverage ceiling | **₹21,000/month** gross (₹25,000 for PwD) | Employee exits ESI when gross crosses ₹21,000 — but only at a contribution-period boundary | ESI (Central) Rules r.50 **[Verified]** |
| Employee contribution | **0.75%** of gross wages | Rounded up to next rupee per employee | ESI Act; rate w.e.f. 01.07.2019 **[Verified]** |
| Employer contribution | **3.25%** of gross wages | Combined **4.00%** | ESI notification 01.07.2019 **[Verified]** |
| Low-wage employee exemption | Employees with **average daily wage ≤ ₹176** are exempt from the *employee* 0.75% share | Employer still pays its 3.25% share for such employees | ESI (Central) Rules r.52; notification 22.09.2019 **[Verified]** |

**What "wages" means for ESI — wider than PF, with its own edge cases.** The ESI
base is **gross**: basic + DA + HRA + conveyance + overtime + city-compensatory +
incentives *paid at intervals not exceeding two months*. Excluded: annual bonus,
gratuity, retrenchment compensation, encashment of leave on discharge, and any
payment made at intervals **exceeding two months** (e.g., a quarterly incentive).
Overtime is included **for contribution** but excluded **for the coverage test** —
so overtime cannot push a ₹20,000 base employee out of coverage, yet ESI is still
charged on the overtime once covered. (Source: ESI Act s.2(22); ESIC instructions on
OT) **[Verified]** This dual treatment of overtime is a named test vector (§06.14).

**The contribution-period rule is the ESI trap.** ESI runs two fixed
**contribution periods** — **April–September** and **October–March** — with
corresponding benefit periods. An employee whose wage crosses ₹21,000 mid-period
**continues to contribute until the end of that contribution period**; they do
not exit ESI mid-period. A payroll engine that drops the employee the month their
wage crosses the ceiling files a wrong return. The exit is period-boundary-aligned,
not month-aligned. **[Verified]** (ESI Central Rules r.50 proviso)

Worked example: an employee at ₹20,000 gross gets a raise to ₹23,000 effective
**1 July**. Because July falls inside the April–September contribution period, ESI
(both shares) continues on the **full ₹23,000** — not ₹21,000 — through September,
and the employee exits ESI only from **1 October**. Contribution is on actual gross,
uncapped, once the employee is in the period; the ₹21,000 is a coverage gate, not a
contribution cap. **[Verified]**



**Figure 38. Esi Contribution Period State Machine**

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    direction TB
    [*] --> NotCovered

    NotCovered: Not covered
    NotCovered: gross > Rs 21,000 at entry (Rs 25,000 PwD)

    Covered: Covered / contributing
    Covered: 0.75 pct employee + 3.25 pct employer on FULL gross
    Covered: contribution uncapped once in period
    Covered: ceiling is a coverage gate, not a contribution cap

    LatchedToBoundary: Ceiling crossed mid-period
    LatchedToBoundary: gross > Rs 21,000, but stays IN
    LatchedToBoundary: keeps contributing on actual gross to period end
    LatchedToBoundary: e.g. raise Rs 20k to Rs 23k on 1 Jul -> ESI on full Rs 23k thru Sep

    Exited: Exited ESI
    Exited: exit effective next period boundary (1 Apr or 1 Oct)
    Exited: retains medical benefit to end of period / linked benefit period

    NotCovered --> Covered: gross <= Rs 21,000 (enrol, IP no. + e-Pehchan first)
    Covered --> Covered: within period (Apr-Sep or Oct-Mar), monthly challan by 15th
    Covered --> LatchedToBoundary: wage crosses Rs 21,000 mid-period
    LatchedToBoundary --> LatchedToBoundary: contribute on full gross to period boundary
    LatchedToBoundary --> Exited: reach 30 Sep / 31 Mar boundary
    Exited --> Covered: gross falls <= Rs 21,000 (re-enrol next period)
    Exited --> [*]

    note right of Covered
        Contribution period -> lagged benefit period
        Apr-Sep contrib -> next Jan-Jun benefit
        Oct-Mar contrib -> next Jul-Dec benefit
    end note

    note left of LatchedToBoundary
        THE ESI TRAP: do NOT drop the member
        the month wage crosses the ceiling.
        Exit is period-boundary-aligned, not month-aligned.
    end note
```


**Contribution period maps to a lagged benefit period — and coverage does not end at
the last working day.** Each contribution period feeds a fixed **benefit period**
after a gap: contributions in **April–September** entitle the IP to benefits in the
following **January–June**, and **October–March** contributions feed the following
**July–December**. This lag is why the period-boundary exit rule matters — dropping a
member a month early can cost them a benefit period they had already funded. Two
further edge cases the coverage engine must hold: (a) an IP who leaves employment
mid-period generally **retains medical benefit** for themselves and family to the end
of the period (and, on satisfying the contributory condition, into the linked benefit
period); and (b) on cessation of insurable employment an IP and spouse can continue
**medical benefit for a further period on payment** of a nominal contribution
(superannuation/retirement continuation). These are not payroll-line items but they
depend on an accurate contribution ledger, so the same data the ECR-equivalent
consumes must persist beyond exit. (Source: ESI Act ss.2(6A), 46; ESI (Central)
Rules on benefit periods and continuation) **[Verified]**

**Filing cadence.**

- **Monthly contribution** — challan generated on the ESIC portal, due by the
  **15th** of the following month.
- **Return of contributions** — the half-yearly return (Forms 5/6) is now largely
  auto-generated from monthly filings, but the engine must reconcile the two
  contribution periods and produce the register.
- **Accident reporting** — Form 12 / IP accident report within prescribed time on
  any employment injury.
- **Enrolment** — new employees get an **IP (Insured Person) number** and e-Pehchan;
  a Temporary Identity Certificate (TIC) is issued pending the permanent card.
  Enrolment must precede the first contribution or the challan rejects the member.

**Penalties.** Interest at **12% p.a.** on delayed contribution, plus damages
graded **5%–25% p.a.** by delay duration (ESI (Central) Rules r.31A/31C).
Non-payment is recoverable as arrears of land revenue and carries prosecution
exposure u/s 85. **[Verified]**

**Data required.** Gross wages (ESI base = gross, which *includes* HRA,
conveyance, overtime — the opposite of the PF/gratuity base, see §06.10), IP number
and e-Pehchan status, average daily wage (for the ₹176 employee-exemption),
contribution-period membership state, dispensary/branch office, PwD flag (₹25,000
ceiling), and the ₹21,000 coverage flag evaluated at period boundaries.

**Product implication.** ESI challan is a P0 filing (§01). The engine needs a
distinct **gross-wage base** concurrent with the PF base, a **contribution-period
state machine** that holds an employee in ESI to the period boundary after they
cross the ceiling, the **₹176 average-daily-wage employee-exemption branch**, the
overtime "include-for-contribution / exclude-for-coverage" split, and rupee-rounding
per employee. **The ESI regime's fate after 22 November 2026 is unresolved** (§06.9) —
this is a payroll-correctness blocker, not a nicety, and is on the validation gate.

### 06.4 Professional Tax — the state patchwork

**What it is.** A tax on professions, trades and employments levied by **states
(and some municipal bodies)** under Article 276 of the Constitution, which caps
the total PT any person pays at **₹2,500 per year**. It is deducted by the employer
from the employee's salary and remitted to the state.

**Who it binds.** Employers in **states that levy PT** — it is not universal.
States with PT include Maharashtra, Karnataka, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Andhra
Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Kerala, Assam, Odisha, Bihar,
Jharkhand, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Tripura, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Puducherry
(list approximate). States that **do not** levy PT include Delhi, Haryana, Uttar
Pradesh, Rajasthan, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab (historically), Goa,
and the union territories other than Puducherry. **[Hypothesis]** — the exact
levy/no-levy list drifts (Punjab introduced a development-tax variant; municipal
PT exists in some states; some states have suspended collection in specific years) —
**kill criterion: the levy status of every state must be verified against the
state's own PT Act/notification, not an aggregator, before it drives a deduction**
(see the dataset dependency below).

**Two registrations, two liabilities — PTEC and PTRC.** A subtlety worth
first-classing: PT has **two** components.

- **PTEC (Professional Tax Enrolment Certificate)** — the *entity's own* PT
  liability (the company/LLP/partnership pays a flat annual PT for itself, e.g.
  ₹2,500/year in Maharashtra), independent of employees.
- **PTRC (Professional Tax Registration Certificate)** — the employer's registration
  to **deduct and remit** PT from employees' salaries.

A single-director private company with no other employees still needs PTEC and pays
the entity PT; a company with staff needs both. The engine must track both numbers
and both liabilities per state. Whole-time directors' remuneration is itself subject
to employee PT. **[Verified]** (state PT Acts; e.g. MH PT Act 1975 ss.3, 5)

**Thresholds, slabs and cadence — this is genuinely per-state.** PT has no
national slab. Each state sets its own income slabs, amounts, gender variants,
and filing frequency. The Article 276 ₹2,500/year ceiling is the only common
constant.

| State | Illustrative slab (monthly) | Filing frequency | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Maharashtra** | Nil ≤ ₹7,500 (men) / ≤ ₹25,000 (women); ₹175 up to ₹10,000; ₹200/month above, **₹300 in February** (to make ₹2,500/yr) | Monthly if PT liability ≥ ₹1L/yr, else annual | MH PT Act 1975 **[Hypothesis]** — verify current slab & the female exemption threshold |
| **Karnataka** | Nil ≤ ₹25,000; **₹200/month** above ₹25,000 | Monthly (20th) | KA PT Act 1976; slab revised FY2023-24 **[Hypothesis]** |
| **West Bengal** | Graded to ₹200/month; ₹2,500/yr cap | Monthly / annual by liability | WB PT Act 1979 **[Hypothesis]** |
| **Tamil Nadu** | Half-yearly slabs (municipal, set by each corporation) | Half-yearly | TN Municipal Acts **[Hypothesis]** |
| **Telangana** | ₹200/month above ₹20,000 (₹150 for ₹15,001–20,000) | Monthly (10th) | **Verified across both research rounds** — the only fully-verified state **[Verified]** |
| **Gujarat** | ₹200/month above ₹12,000 | Monthly | GJ PT Act 1976 **[Hypothesis]** |

Worked example (Karnataka, employee gross ₹40,000/month): above the ₹25,000
threshold, PT = **₹200/month × 12 = ₹2,400/year**, deducted monthly, remitted by the
20th. Worked example of the **Maharashtra February quirk**: a Maharashtra employee
above ₹10,000 pays ₹200 for eleven months and **₹300 in February**, totalling exactly
₹2,500 — the Article 276 ceiling. An engine that applies a flat ₹200 for all twelve
months **under-deducts by ₹100** and the annual reconciliation fails; the February
top-up is not a rounding artefact, it is the statute engineering the ₹2,500 cap.
**[Hypothesis]** — verify the current Maharashtra February amount before it drives a
deduction.

**Penalties.** State-specific: typically interest (1.25%–2%/month) on late
payment plus a penalty for late registration/return; some states levy a flat
per-return late fee. Must be modelled per-state. **[Hypothesis]** — verify each
state's penalty schedule against its own PT Act.

**Data required.** Employee's **work state** (not residence — PT follows the place
of employment, which matters for remote/multi-state workforces), monthly gross/PT
wage, gender (some states have female-favourable thresholds), and the state's
registration numbers (PTEC for the entity, PTRC for the employee deductions). For a
remote employee, "work state" is a policy decision the engine must capture explicitly
— it is a live ambiguity for distributed teams and cannot be inferred from the
employer's HQ. **[Hypothesis]** — the correct PT situs for a fully-remote employee is
unsettled; **kill criterion: obtain a state-level position (or a conservative
deduct-at-employer-registered-state policy) before filing for remote staff.**

**Product implication.** This is a **maintained-dataset problem**, not a
feature-cleverness problem. Frappe HR already ships PT across 15+ states free and
open-source, so **multi-state PT carries zero differentiation credit** (§05,
Killed). Draft 1's validation plan flags the entire PT dataset as **undone work
and a build dependency**: only Telangana is verified; aggregator PT tables are
"materially disputed" and "at least one widely-cited 2026 table reproduces a
superseded structure." The requirement is therefore twofold: (a) build a
**per-state, effective-dated PT rule table** — levy y/n, slabs, gender variants,
periodicity, PTEC/PTRC registration, filing frequency, February/annual top-up
quirks, effective dates — sourced from each state's own Act/notification; and (b)
treat it as permanent statutory-maintenance load (§13), not a one-time seed. The
differentiation is the *maintained SLA on this table*, not its existence.

---

### 06.5 TDS on salary (u/s 192) and the 24Q → Form 138 breaking change

**What it is.** The employer's obligation to deduct income tax at source from
salary under **s.192**, deposit it monthly, file a quarterly statement, and issue
an annual certificate. This binds from **employee one** — no threshold.

**Who it binds.** Every employer paying taxable salary, from the first rupee of
tax liability. The employer must compute each employee's projected annual tax
(under the regime the employee elects — new default regime u/s 115BAC vs old
regime), spread it across the remaining months, and true-up.

**The two-regime computation.** Since the new regime became the **default** under
s.115BAC, the engine must compute tax under **both regimes per employee**, honour
the employee's election (and its default-if-silent behaviour), and re-project on
every declaration change. The new-regime slabs, the standard deduction (₹75,000 in
the new regime from FY2024-25), the old-regime Chapter VI-A deductions, and the
s.87A rebate all differ. This is a per-employee, per-period recomputation, and it
interacts with mid-year joiners carrying previous-employer income (Form 12B).

Illustrative new-regime slabs (**FY2025-26 / AY2026-27**, as the worked base):

| Slab (annual taxable income) | Rate | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Up to ₹4,00,000 | Nil | Finance Act 2025, s.115BAC(1A) **[Verified]** |
| ₹4,00,001 – ₹8,00,000 | 5% | " |
| ₹8,00,001 – ₹12,00,000 | 10% | " |
| ₹12,00,001 – ₹16,00,000 | 15% | " |
| ₹16,00,001 – ₹20,00,000 | 20% | " |
| ₹20,00,001 – ₹24,00,000 | 25% | " |
| Above ₹24,00,000 | 30% | " |

s.87A rebate makes income up to **₹12,00,000** effectively tax-free in the new
regime for FY2025-26 (rebate up to ₹60,000), with **marginal relief** just above
₹12L so the extra tax cannot exceed the extra income. **[Verified]** These figures
are a **worked base, not a constant** — the current-FY slabs, standard deduction and
rebate ceiling must be effective-dated against the latest Finance Act. **[Hypothesis]**
— for FY2026-27 (the current running year) **kill criterion: verify slabs, rebate
ceiling and standard deduction against Finance Act 2026 / the Budget 2026 notification
and any corrigendum before running the year's TDS.**

Worked two-regime example (FY2025-26, salaried, gross ₹15,00,000; declared old-regime
deductions: 80C ₹1,50,000, 80D ₹25,000, HRA exempt ₹1,00,000):

| | New regime | Old regime |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gross salary | ₹15,00,000 | ₹15,00,000 |
| Standard deduction | ₹75,000 | ₹50,000 |
| HRA / Chapter VI-A | — | ₹1,00,000 + ₹1,75,000 |
| Taxable income | ₹14,25,000 | ₹11,75,000 |
| Tax before cess | ₹93,750 | ₹1,65,000 (old slabs) |
| Cess 4% | ₹3,750 | ₹6,600 |
| **Annual tax** | **₹97,500** | **₹1,71,600** |

Here the new regime wins by ~₹74,100 — but flip the deductions up (large 80C + home-
loan interest u/s 24(b) + NPS 80CCD(1B)) and the old regime wins. The engine must run
both **every time a declaration changes** and surface the cheaper one, while honouring
the employee's actual election. Old-regime slabs and surcharge (10% >₹50L, 15% >₹1Cr,
25% >₹2Cr; the 37% band is removed and surcharge capped at 25% in the new regime) plus
**marginal relief at each surcharge threshold** are all in scope. **[Verified]**

**Cadence.**

| Filing | Frequency | Due date | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TDS deposit (challan) | Monthly | **7th** of following month (30 April for March) | IT Rules r.30 **[Verified]** |
| Quarterly statement (24Q / **Form 138**) | Quarterly | 31 Jul (Q1), 31 Oct (Q2), 31 Jan (Q3), 31 May (Q4) | IT Rules r.31A **[Verified]** |
| Annual certificate (Form 16 / **Form 130**) | Annual | 15 June following FY | IT Rules r.31 **[Verified]** |

**The breaking file-format change — this is a build-critical event.** Draft 1
established it as Verified and it is reproduced here as the register entry:

> **Form 138 replaces Form 24Q, and the record layout is a breaking change.**
> - Challan sub-headings **301–312 remap to A–K, with 303 deleted**.
> - Annexure I fields **313–327 remap to C–N, with 313, 321, 322 and 325 removed**.
> - **Surcharge, Education Cess and Penalty/Others are deleted**; **Interest
>   Allocation and Others Allocation are added**.
> - **Q1–Q3 v1.2 shipped 22 July 2026**; correction-statement structures were
>   published **4 August 2026**.
> - **The Q4 regular file format does not exist yet.** Q4's annexure feeds
>   **Form 130 (ex-Form 16) Part B**, so the annual certificate cannot be fully
>   built until the Q4 layout lands.
>
> (Source: CBDT / TIN-NSDL RPU & FVU release notes, 22 Jul 2026 and 4 Aug 2026) **[Verified]**

**Two newer declaration forms the engine must consume.**

- **Form 12BB** — employee's declaration of HRA, LTA, home-loan interest and
  Chapter VI-A claims, with proofs, for the employer to grant during the year.
  (Source: IT Rules r.26C) **[Verified]**
- **Form 12BAA** — introduced 01.10.2024, lets an employee report **other TDS/TCS**
  (e.g., TCS on a car purchase, TDS on interest) to the employer so it is netted
  against salary TDS, reducing over-deduction. The engine should accept and apply it.
  (Source: Finance (No.2) Act 2024; CBDT notification Oct 2024) **[Verified]**

**Arrears relief u/s 89(1) / Form 10E — the retro-run's tax twin.** When salary
arrears are paid in a later year (a raise backdated, a pay-commission-style
settlement, or the §06.10 retro-recompute paying out), the lump sum can push the
employee into a higher slab in the year of receipt. Section 89(1) relief re-spreads
the arrears to the years they relate to and taxes them at those years' rates, claimed
via **Form 10E** (which must be filed before the return or the relief is denied).
Because the spine already recomputes wages against the *period's* rule version for
PF/ESI (R3), the same arrears event must carry its **year-of-accrual attribution**
into TDS so 89(1) relief can be computed — a payroll arrears line is simultaneously a
PF retro, an ESI retro and a potential 89(1) event. (Source: IT Act s.89; Rule 21A;
Form 10E) **[Verified]**

**Penalties.**

| Failure | Consequence | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Late deposit of deducted tax | Interest **1.5%/month** (or part) from deduction to deposit | IT Act s.201(1A) **[Verified]** |
| Non-deduction | Interest **1%/month** from due-to-deduct to actual deduction; disallowance risk | s.201(1A) **[Verified]** |
| Late filing of statement | **₹200/day** u/s 234E (capped at TDS amount) | s.234E **[Verified]** |
| Non/late filing penalty | ₹10,000–₹1,00,000 u/s 271H | s.271H **[Verified]** |
| Late issue of certificate | ₹100/day u/s 272A(2)(g) | s.272A **[Verified]** |

**Inoperative PAN — a per-employee higher-rate branch.** Where an employee's PAN is
**inoperative** (Aadhaar not linked), TDS on salary is deducted at the **higher of
the applicable rate or 20%** u/s 206AA, and no lower-rate benefit applies. Note that
s.206AB (higher TDS for non-filers) **does not apply to salary** — a common
mis-implementation; s.192 is expressly excluded. So the only higher-rate branch for
salary is the inoperative-PAN 206AA path. (Source: s.206AA; s.206AB(1) proviso
excluding s.192; CBDT circular on inoperative PAN) **[Verified]**

**Data required.** PAN (valid, operative/Aadhaar-linked — an inoperative PAN
triggers the 206AA higher rate), regime election, Form 12BB investment declarations
and proofs, Form 12BAA other-TDS/TCS, previous-employer income (Form 12B),
perquisite values (incl. the meal/voucher thresholds — ₹200/meal and ₹15,000/yr
vouchers from 01.04.2026, §11 of Draft 1), HRA/LTA claims, and challan/CIN
reconciliation.

**Product implication.** Form 138 generation is a **P0 filing** and its layout is
**versioned and effective-dated by quarter** — Q1–Q3 on the v1.2 layout, Q4 on a
layout that does not yet exist. The engine must: (a) not hard-code field numbers
(301–312 etc.) but map them through a versioned schema; (b) compute tax under both
regimes with surcharge and marginal relief; (c) reconcile challans (CIN) against
deducted amounts before file generation; (d) gate Form 130 Part B on the arrival of
the Q4 layout; (e) handle inoperative-PAN 206AA higher-rate deduction (and *not*
mis-apply 206AB to salary); and (f) consume Form 12BB and Form 12BAA. The
statutory-change watcher (§13) must be **watching for the Q4 layout release
specifically** — it is a named, expected, dated dependency.

### 06.6 Gratuity

**What it is.** A lump-sum terminal benefit payable to an employee on exit after
qualifying service, funded by the employer. It is both a **payout obligation** on
exit and an **accruing liability** the employer must account for continuously.

**Who it binds.** Establishments with **10 or more** employees (latches on the
preceding-twelve-months test). Payable on resignation, retirement, death or
disablement after **5 years of continuous service** — the 5-year condition is
**waived on death or disablement**.

**What "continuous service" means — the 240-day rule.** "Five years" is not five
calendar years of daily attendance. Under s.2A, an employee who has actually worked
**240 days in a twelve-month period** (190 days for below-ground mines or a
five-day-week establishment) is deemed in continuous service for that year. Leave,
LOP, lay-off, legal strike and maternity leave count toward continuity; the fifth
year is satisfied at **4 years + 240 days** per several High Court rulings (Madras
HC, *Mettur Beardsell*). (Source: POG Act s.2A) **[Verified]** — the "4 years 240
days = eligible" reading is followed by some HCs but not uniformly settled across all
jurisdictions; **[Hypothesis]** — **kill criterion: confirm the controlling
jurisdiction's position before auto-approving a claim at exactly 4y240d.**

**Computation.**

| Item | Rule | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Formula (covered employee) | **(15/26) × last-drawn monthly wages × completed years of service** | Payment of Gratuity Act s.4 **[Verified]** |
| Seasonal establishment | **7 days' wages** for each season | POG Act s.4(2) proviso **[Verified]** |
| "Wages" for gratuity | Basic + DA (and, under the Codes, the s.2(88) wage definition with the 50% add-back — §06.10) | POG Act s.2(s); CoSS s.2(88) **[Verified]** |
| Rounding of service | ≥ 6 months in the final year rounds up to a full year | POG Act s.4 **[Verified]** |
| Tax-exemption ceiling | **₹20,00,000** lifetime, cumulative across all employers (s.10(10)) | CBDT notification 2019 **[Verified]** |

Worked example: last-drawn Basic+DA ₹52,000, 7 years 8 months service (rounds to
8). Gratuity = (15/26) × 52,000 × 8 = **₹2,40,000**. Tax-free (below ₹20L ceiling).
Contrast: 7 years **4 months** rounds **down** to 7 → (15/26) × 52,000 × 7 =
**₹2,10,000**. The 6-month boundary is a hard test vector (§06.14); an engine that
rounds 7y4m up over-pays and mis-states the accrued liability.

**Forfeiture.** Gratuity is not unconditional. Under s.4(6) it may be forfeited
**wholly** where services are terminated for an act of violence, or an offence
involving moral turpitude committed in the course of employment; and **to the extent
of damage/loss** caused by the employee's wilful act. The engine must support a
forfeiture flag with a reason code on the exit record, not silently pay. (Source:
POG Act s.4(6)) **[Verified]**

**Compulsory insurance (s.4A).** The 2018 amendment made it obligatory for employers
(other than government and those with an approved gratuity fund) to obtain gratuity
insurance from LIC or an IRDAI-registered insurer; enforcement is via **state
notification** and several states (e.g., Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka) have
notified rules. **[Hypothesis]** — s.4A is not uniformly enforced across states;
**kill criterion: verify whether the tenant's state has notified s.4A compulsory
insurance before representing it as a live obligation.**

**Cadence.** No periodic filing, but: (a) the employer must display an abstract
and maintain nomination (Form F); (b) on a claim, payment is due **within 30 days**
of it becoming payable, with **simple interest** for delay beyond 30 days; and
(c) the **accruing liability** should be actuarially estimated for the books
(AS 15 / Ind AS 19) and, where the employer runs an approved gratuity fund
(e.g., LIC group gratuity), contributions are periodic.

**Penalties.** Delay in payment beyond 30 days attracts interest at the notified
rate; non-payment can attract fine/imprisonment u/s 9. **[Verified]**

**Data required.** Continuous-service ledger (including how leave, LOP, lay-off and
strikes affect the 240-day test), last-drawn wages under the correct definition,
nomination (Form F), date and cause of exit (to apply the death/disablement waiver
and any forfeiture), and cumulative gratuity received from prior employers (for the
₹20L lifetime exemption).

**Product implication.** Two distinct features: (1) a **gratuity payout calculator**
on exit that applies the 5-year/240-day rule, the death/disablement waiver, the
6-month rounding, forfeiture and the ₹20L cumulative exemption; and (2) a **running
accrual ledger** per employee so the liability is always current for the books. §01
lists gratuity among the statutory computations the engine must own; the accrual side
is what separates a payroll tool from a spreadsheet.

---

### 06.7 Payment of Bonus

**What it is.** A statutory profit-linked bonus, distinct from any discretionary or
performance bonus. It is an **annual** liability computed on allocable surplus, with
a statutory floor and cap, that the engine must accrue through the year and pay after
the accounts close. It is a genuine gap if omitted: it binds at the same 20-headcount
threshold as EPF and sits squarely in the beachhead.

**Who it binds.** Factories, and every establishment employing **20 or more** persons
on any day in the accounting year. Two latching subtleties: (a) the appropriate
government may **notify establishments with 10–19 persons** into coverage, so the
trigger is not uniformly 20 in every state; and (b) once the Act applies, it
**continues to apply even if headcount later falls below 20** (s.1(5)) — the classic
"once covered, always covered" latch that §06.1's step function must encode.
Eligible: employees drawing wages **≤ ₹21,000/month** who have worked **at least 30
working days** in the accounting year. (Source: Payment of Bonus Act 1965 ss.1(3),
1(5), 8; eligibility ceiling ₹21,000 by the 2015 amendment, effective FY 2014-15)
**[Verified]**

**Computation.**

| Item | Rule | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eligibility wage ceiling | **₹21,000/month** | POB Act s.2(13), 2015 amendment **[Verified]** |
| Minimum bonus | **8.33%** of bonus wages (payable even in a loss year, subject to infancy exemption) | POB Act s.10 **[Verified]** |
| Maximum bonus | **20%** of bonus wages | POB Act s.11 **[Verified]** |
| Calculation ceiling | Bonus computed on **min(actual wage, ₹7,000 or the minimum wage for the scheduled employment, whichever higher)** | POB Act s.12, 2015 amendment **[Verified]** |
| Set-on / set-off | Allocable surplus above max carries forward, deficit carries forward, up to **4 years** | POB Act s.15 **[Verified]** |
| Infancy exemption | New establishments exempt from bonus for the **first 5 accounting years** except in years they profit | POB Act s.16 **[Verified]** |

Worked example: employee wages ₹18,000/month (eligible, ≤₹21,000); the scheduled
minimum wage for the role is ₹10,000/month, which is higher than ₹7,000, so the
**calculation ceiling is ₹10,000**. Minimum bonus = 8.33% × ₹10,000 × 12 =
**₹9,996/year**; maximum = 20% × ₹10,000 × 12 = **₹24,000/year**. Note the employee's
actual ₹18,000 wage is **not** the bonus base — the s.12 ceiling caps it at ₹10,000.
An engine that computes bonus on actual wage over-pays and mis-accrues; one that uses
a flat ₹7,000 without checking the higher minimum wage under-pays. **[Verified]**

**Cadence and filing.** Bonus is payable **within 8 months of the close of the
accounting year** — for an April–March year, by **30 November**. The employer files
**Form D** (annual return) to the labour department, and maintains Forms A/B/C
(allocable surplus, set-on/set-off, bonus disbursed). (Source: Payment of Bonus
Rules 1975, r.4–5) **[Verified]**

**Penalties.** Contravention attracts imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to
₹1,000 (or both) u/s 28. **[Verified]**

**Interaction with the other statutes.** Statutory bonus is **excluded** from the
PF/gratuity add-back base and from the ESI wage base (it is an annual payment at
intervals exceeding two months, §06.3). It **is** taxable salary for TDS (§06.5) in
the year of receipt. So the same bonus amount is invisible to ECR/ESI but visible to
Form 138 — a routing rule the wage engine must encode, not a single "bonus" field.

**Product implication.** Bonus is (a) an **accrual** through the year for the books
and (b) an **annual payout + Form D filing** after accounts close. The engine must
apply the ₹21,000 eligibility gate, the s.12 calculation ceiling (with the
minimum-wage lookup per scheduled employment and state), the 8.33%–20% band with
set-on/set-off carry-forward, and the infancy exemption for new establishments.
**[Hypothesis]** — under the **Code on Wages 2019 (ss.26–41)** the bonus provisions
are subsumed and the eligibility/calculation ceilings become notified variables;
**kill criterion: verify whether the Code-era bonus ceilings have been notified (and
supersede ₹21,000/₹7,000) before computing bonus for any post-21.11.2025 accounting
year.** Effective-date the ceilings like every other rate.

### 06.8 Labour Welfare Fund (LWF)

**What it is.** A small statutory welfare contribution to a **state** Labour
Welfare Fund, split between employee and employer, funding worker welfare
activities. Like PT, it is a **state-by-state patchwork** — levied only where a
state has an LWF Act.

**Who it binds.** Employers in states with an LWF Act (approximately 14–16 states),
for employees below a defined wage/designation threshold. States with LWF include
Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Gujarat, Kerala,
Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Delhi, Haryana, Punjab, West Bengal, Goa. States
without: Uttar Pradesh (no active LWF), Rajasthan, Bihar, and most north-eastern
states. **[Hypothesis]** — Frappe HR ships LWF across 14 states, corroborating the
count — **kill criterion: verify each state's LWF applicability, amount and
periodicity against the state LWF Act/notification before it drives a deduction.**

**Thresholds, amounts and cadence — per state.**

| State | Employee / employer contribution | Frequency | Source cue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Maharashtra** | ₹25 (emp) + ₹75 (employer) for wages > ₹3,000; lower slab below | **Half-yearly** (Jun & Dec) | MH LWF Act 1953 **[Hypothesis]** |
| **Karnataka** | ₹20 (emp) + ₹40 (employer) | **Annual** (Dec) | KA LWF Act 1965 **[Hypothesis]** |
| **Tamil Nadu** | ₹20 (emp) + ₹40 (employer) | Annual (Dec) | TN LWF Act 1972 **[Hypothesis]** |
| **Gujarat** | ₹6 (emp) + ₹12 (employer) | Half-yearly (Jun & Dec) | GJ LWF Act 1953 **[Hypothesis]** |
| **Delhi** | ₹0.75 (emp) + ₹2.25 (employer) | Half-yearly | DL LWF Act **[Hypothesis]** |

The point of the table is not the exact rupee values (which are small and drift)
but the **structural diversity**: amount, employee/employer split, wage threshold
and periodicity (monthly / half-yearly / annual) all vary by state. The
deduction/remittance calendar therefore differs per state, per period. A named trap:
some states levy LWF on the employee **only in the deduction month** (e.g., the
December cycle), so a naive "deduct every month" rule over-collects — the periodicity
is part of the rule, not a display detail. **[Hypothesis]** — verify the deduction
month per state.

**Penalties.** State-specific interest and penalty on delayed remittance; generally
minor in rupee terms but a compliance flag. **[Hypothesis]** — verify per state.

**Data required.** Work state, wage/designation eligibility, employee/employer
split, and the state's remittance periodicity and deduction month.

**Product implication.** Same shape as PT: a **maintained, effective-dated,
per-state rule table** feeding the deduction engine and the filing calendar, and
part of the permanent statutory-maintenance load. **No differentiation credit** —
Frappe ships it free. The value is the maintained SLA, and the LWF + PT datasets
together are the single largest "undone but cheap" build dependency named in the
Draft 1 validation plan.

### 06.9 The four Labour Codes and the November 2026 cliff

**What they are.** Four consolidating Codes replacing 29 central labour laws:
the **Code on Wages 2019**, the **Industrial Relations Code 2020**, the **Code on
Social Security 2020 (CoSS)**, and the **Occupational Safety, Health and Working
Conditions Code 2020 (OSH&WC)**.

**Status — settled, not draft.** The four Codes came into force **21 November 2025**,
and final Central Rules under all four were notified **8 May 2026**. Draft 1
corrects an earlier framing: the story is **not** "be the guide through chaos," it
is **"build against a settled spec."** (Source: MoLE gazette, force-date 21.11.2025;
Central Rules 08.05.2026) **[Verified]**

The residual uncertainty is **state divergence**, not central uncertainty. State
rules under the Codes are notifying **unevenly across states** (labour is on the
Concurrent List, so each state notifies its own rules and thresholds), so a
multi-state employer can hit conflicting state and central positions on the same
question — overtime spread, wage-period, register format. The data model must
**assume divergence** — effective-dated rules per state from v1 — rather than treat
it as an exception (Draft 1 risk register). **[Verified]**

**What the Codes change for payroll, concretely.** Beyond the wage-definition
add-back (§06.10), the notified Rules fix: a **wage period not exceeding one month**;
**wages payable by the 7th** of the following month (with tighter deadlines for
weekly/fortnightly-paid workers); **overtime at twice the ordinary rate** with a
**quarterly ceiling of 144 OT hours**; a prescribed **appointment letter** for every
employee; and the collapse of dozens of registers into **four consolidated registers**
(employees, wages, attendance/leave, and a muster) in electronic form with five-year
retention. Each of these is a payroll-engine or document-generation requirement.
(Source: Code on Wages Central Rules 2026; OSH&WC Central Rules 2026) **[Verified]**

#### The November 2026 cliff

This is the single most time-critical item in the register, and the one the
standing "check for a corrigendum" rule exists because of.

- **The EPF Act 1952 is repealed with effect from 21 November 2025.** **[Verified]**
- **CoSS s.164(2)(b)** saves the **EPF Scheme 1952, EDLI 1976, EPS 1995 and all
  ESI rules and schemes for one year** — expiring on or about **21 November 2026**.
  **[Verified]**
- **The EPF side has a named successor:** the **Employees' Provident Funds Scheme,
  2026**, with **12% re-notified retrospectively to 21.11.2025 by S.O. 3582(E)**.
  **Build against Scheme 2026.** **[Verified]**
- **The ESI side is unresolved.** There is no confirmed successor instrument for
  the ESI schemes after the one-year saving lapses. This is a **payroll-engine
  correctness blocker** that needs a primary-source answer before the date.
  **[Hypothesis]** — **kill criterion: monitor ESIC and MoLE notifications; if no
  successor/extension is notified before ~21 Nov 2026, ESI computation post-cliff
  is undefined and must be escalated, not guessed.** (Draft 1 validation gate #8.)

> **Trap for anyone re-verifying (reproduced verbatim from Draft 1 because it is
> load-bearing):** indiacode.nic.in's bare-Act footnote still reproduces the
> uncorrected **S.O. 5319(E)** enumeration. Verifying against indiacode or the
> original gazette alone reproduces this exact error — which is how one research
> round concluded the opposite. **The corrigendum must be checked.** **[Verified]**

**Product implication.** (a) The PF engine is built against **Scheme 2026** with
the 12% as a notified variable. (b) The ESI post-cliff behaviour is an open item
tracked on the validation gate, and the statutory-change watcher must be keyed to
**catch amendments and corrigenda, not just new instruments** (Draft 1, §13) —
a watcher keyed only to new notifications would have missed the corrigendum that
inverted the entire November 2026 analysis. (c) State-rule divergence under the
Codes is a first-class effective-dated dimension, not an exception path.

---

### 06.10 The wage-definition problem — the hardest single calculation

This is not a separate statute; it is the **shared base** that re-computes EPF,
gratuity, bonus and more under the Codes. Draft 1 flags it as "the hardest single
calculation in the build," and it belongs in the spine because it silently
re-bases half the other entries in this section.

**The 50% add-back rule.** Identical text in **Code on Wages s.2(y)** and **Code
on Social Security s.2(88)**: "wages" excludes certain components (HRA, conveyance,
bonus, overtime, commission, employer PF/pension contribution, etc.), **but if the
sum of excluded components exceeds one-half of all remuneration, the excess over 50%
is deemed to be wages and added back**. This prevents employers from suppressing the
PF/gratuity base by loading pay into allowances. **[Verified]**

**Consequence — multiple concurrent wage bases on one payslip.**

- The **add-back base** (for PF, gratuity, bonus-adjacent computations) *excludes*
  conveyance, HRA, award settlements and overtime — then adds back any excess over
  50%.
- The **equal-pay / payment-of-wages base** *includes* those same components.
- **ESI's gross base** (§06.3) is a third, wider still.
- The **bonus base** (§06.7) is a fourth, capped at ₹7,000/minimum-wage.

So the engine needs **at least four concurrent wage computations per employee, per
period**. A single "wage" field is a design error, and the wrong choice of base is
the single most common source of a materially wrong filing.

**"Or such other per cent as may be notified."** The statute makes the 50% a
**standing notified variable**, not a constant. This is the permanent justification
for effective-dating the wage-definition rule, independent of any transitional
argument. **[Verified]**

**Requirement (verbatim from Draft 1, because it is a hard acceptance criterion):**
the wage-definition rule must be **versioned, effective-dated, and retrospectively
recomputable with an audit trail. Arrears and retro runs must recompute against
the rule version in force for the period being corrected, not the version in force
today.**

Worked illustration of the add-back. Monthly CTC ₹1,00,000 structured as Basic
₹35,000, HRA ₹20,000, conveyance ₹10,000, special allowance ₹35,000. Excluded
components (HRA + conveyance + special, treating special as excludable) = ₹65,000 =
65% of ₹1,00,000. Half of remuneration = ₹50,000. Excess over 50% = ₹15,000, **added
back to wages**. PF wage base becomes ₹35,000 + ₹15,000 = ₹50,000 (then capped at
₹15,000 ceiling for statutory PF, or actual if the employer opts in). The add-back
materially raises the gratuity base (which has **no** ceiling) even where the PF
₹15,000 ceiling absorbs it — which is exactly why gratuity and PF cannot share one
base field.

Counter-case (no add-back triggers): Basic ₹55,000, HRA ₹22,000, conveyance ₹8,000,
special ₹15,000 on the same ₹1,00,000. Excluded = ₹45,000 = 45% < 50%, so **no
add-back**; the PF/gratuity base is the ₹55,000 basic (capped at ₹15,000 for PF). The
rule is a conditional, evaluated per employee per period against that period's
structure — not a fixed formula.

**Product implication.** The wage engine is the foundation the whole spine sits on:
multiple concurrent bases, effective-dated definitions, retro-recompute against the
period's rule version, full audit trail. Get this wrong and every downstream filing
(ECR, ESI, Form 138, gratuity, bonus) is wrong. This is the single strongest argument
for the "compliance-maintenance operation, not feature-velocity startup" org shape (§13).

### 06.11 The consolidated filing calendar

The obligations above collapse into a recurring calendar. The product's headline
metric is **filings completed on time** (§01), so the calendar is not a report — it
is the operating surface. The dominant monthly rhythm clusters on the **7th and
15th**.



**Figure 39. Filing Calendar**

```mermaid

    EPF ECR + challan - by 15th               :active, epf15, 2025-04-01, 365d
    ESI contribution - by 15th                :active, esi15, 2025-04-01, 365d

```


| Due | Filing | Statute | Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **7th** (30 Apr for March) | TDS challan deposit (s.192) | Income-tax | Monthly |
| **10th** (state-varying) | Professional Tax (e.g., Telangana) | State PT | Monthly (state-varying) |
| **15th** | **EPF ECR** + challan | EPF/Scheme 2026 | Monthly |
| **15th** | **ESI** contribution challan | ESI | Monthly |
| **20th** (state-varying) | PT (e.g., Karnataka) | State PT | Monthly (state-varying) |
| **31 Jul / 31 Oct / 31 Jan / 31 May** | **Form 138** (ex-24Q) quarterly statement | Income-tax | Quarterly |
| **End of Apr & Oct** | ESI contribution-period boundary (coverage re-eval) | ESI | Half-yearly |
| **Jun / Dec (state-varying)** | LWF remittance | State LWF | Half-yearly / annual |
| **30 Nov** (8 months after FY close) | **Bonus payout + Form D** | Payment of Bonus | Annual |
| **15 Jun** | **Form 130** (ex-Form 16) issue | Income-tax | Annual |
| **On exit / within 30 days** | Gratuity payment | POG Act | Event-driven |
| **On the day / period** | New Codes: appointment letter, wage slip, four registers | Labour Codes | Event / continuous |

Three structural facts the calendar must encode:

1. **State-varying due dates.** PT and LWF due dates and frequencies differ by
   state, so a multi-state tenant has multiple parallel calendars. The calendar is
   derived per (tenant × state × obligation), effective-dated.
2. **The quarterly TDS layout is versioned.** Q1–Q3 FY2026-27 file on the Form 138
   v1.2 layout; **Q4 files on a layout that does not exist yet** and gates Form 130
   Part B. The calendar must show Q4 and Form 130 as **blocked-pending-layout**,
   not merely "future."
3. **Annual accruals surface late but must accrue early.** Bonus (30 Nov) and the
   gratuity accrual are annual/continuous liabilities whose *filing* is late in the
   cycle but whose *accrual* runs every period — the calendar must show both the
   accrual cadence and the payout deadline, or the customer is surprised in November.

**Product implication.** A CA-facing console needs this calendar **per client**,
with one-click Form 138 and PT export and read-only audit access (§16, Draft 1).
The four consolidated statutory registers are electronic with **five-year
retention** (§01). The calendar is where "the filing is the unit of delivery"
becomes a screen.

### 06.12 Cross-cutting requirements the spine imposes on the engine

Pulling the above together, the statutory spine dictates the following
non-negotiable engine properties. These are acceptance criteria, not aspirations.

| # | Requirement | Driven by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R1 | **Multiple concurrent wage bases** per employee per period (PF add-back base, gross/ESI base, payment-of-wages base, bonus ₹7,000-capped base) | §06.10, §06.3, §06.7 |
| R2 | **Effective-dated, versioned rules** for every rate, slab, ceiling and definition — 12% PF, 50% add-back, PT/LWF slabs, TDS regimes, bonus ceilings | §06.2, §06.4, §06.7, §06.8, §06.10 |
| R3 | **Retrospective recompute with audit trail** — arrears/retro runs use the rule version in force for the period corrected | §06.10, §06.2 |
| R4 | **Threshold latching** — obligations that trigger on a look-back window stay on when headcount dips, and are explicitly retired, never silently dropped | §06.1 |
| R5 | **Per-state, per-tenant derived filing calendar** — PT/LWF/bonus due dates and frequencies vary | §06.4, §06.8, §06.11 |
| R6 | **Versioned file-format schemas** — Form 138 field-number remaps behind a schema; Q4 layout pluggable when it lands; ECR/ESI layouts likewise | §06.5, §06.2, §06.3 |
| R7 | **Rules-first, LLM-last** — no statutory or monetary figure is ever model-generated | §08 (Verified) |
| R8 | **Corrigendum-aware statutory watcher** — catches amendments and corrigenda, not just new instruments; keyed to named dated dependencies (Q4 layout, ESI cliff) | §06.9, §06.5, §13 |
| R9 | **Pre-filing validation** — UAN KYC state, PAN operative/Aadhaar-link, IP/e-Pehchan, CIN reconciliation surfaced before the window, not after rejection | §06.2, §06.5, §06.3 |
| R10 | **Migration-grade register reproduction** — 3A/6A-equivalent, ESI 5/6, PT/LWF registers, Bonus Forms A–D for Tally/Zoho/Kredily/Frappe import | §06.2, §06.7, §16 |
| R11 | **Engagement-type-aware headcount** — apprentices/NAPS excluded, contract labour and directors handled per rule, for the obligation step function | §06.1 |
| R12 | **Correct income routing of the same rupee** — a statutory bonus is invisible to ECR/ESI but visible to Form 138; the wage engine encodes the routing | §06.7, §06.3, §06.5 |

### 06.14 Statutory test vectors — the golden cases the engine must pass

The spine is only as good as the cases that catch its bugs. These are the named
golden test vectors, each a place a naive engine files a wrong number. They are the
acceptance suite for the compliance engine and should be checked against a primary
source before every rate-change release. **[Verified]** (each derives from the cited
rule above)

| # | Vector | Correct behaviour | Wrong behaviour it catches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TV1 | EPS cap on actual-wage PF election | Employer EPS = ₹1,250 regardless; excess to EPF | 8.33% applied to full wage; pension over-allocated |
| TV2 | EPS closed to post-01.09.2014 high-earner first-joiner | Full 12% employer share to EPF, EPS = 0 | EPS split applied to an ineligible member |
| TV3 | ESI mid-period ceiling crossing (raise to ₹23,000 on 1 Jul) | ESI on full ₹23,000 through Sep; exit 1 Oct | Member dropped in July; wrong return |
| TV4 | ESI ₹176 average-daily-wage employee | Employee 0.75% waived; employer 3.25% still charged | Both shares charged, or both waived |
| TV5 | ESI overtime | Excluded from coverage test; included in contribution | OT pushes member out of coverage, or OT untaxed |
| TV6 | 50% add-back triggers (excluded = 65%) | ₹15,000 excess added back to PF/gratuity base | No add-back; suppressed base |
| TV7 | 50% add-back does not trigger (excluded = 45%) | No add-back | Add-back applied unnecessarily |
| TV8 | Gratuity 6-month rounding (7y8m vs 7y4m) | 7y8m → 8 years; 7y4m → 7 years | Both rounded the same direction |
| TV9 | Bonus s.12 calculation ceiling (wage ₹18,000, min wage ₹10,000) | Base = ₹10,000, not ₹18,000 or ₹7,000 | Bonus on actual wage, or flat ₹7,000 |
| TV10 | Maharashtra PT February top-up | ₹300 in Feb to reach ₹2,500/yr | Flat ₹200×12 = ₹2,400 (₹100 short) |
| TV11 | Inoperative-PAN salary TDS | 206AA higher-of-rate-or-20%; 206AB does *not* apply to salary | 206AB mis-applied, or normal rate on inoperative PAN |
| TV12 | Retro arrears recompute | Recompute against the rule version in force for the corrected period | Recompute at today's rate |
| TV13 | Un-seeded / mismatched UAN at ECR time | Member surfaced to JD/seeding queue before the window; ECR not silently short-credited | "UAN exists" treated as filable; contribution silently uncredited |
| TV14 | Arrears paid in a later year | Attributed to year(s) of accrual for PF/ESI retro and for s.89(1)/Form 10E relief | Whole lump taxed at receipt-year slab; no 89(1) attribution |
| TV15 | ABRY/PMRPY-subsidised member | ECR reports full statutory contribution; employer remittance reduced by subsidised share against live eligibility | Subsidy modelled as a flat rate cut; ECR and remittance mis-stated, or a lapsed scheme carried forward |

**Bottom line for the spine.** The statutory compliance spine is the product.
Every entry here is a deterministic, effective-dated, retrospectively-recomputable
rule feeding a filing, and the filing — ECR, ESI challan, PT return, Form 138,
Form 130, bonus Form D, the four registers — is what the customer pays for. The
competitive position (§01) is honest: this is **parity with Zoho and differentiation
only against Frappe, Kredily and Tally on filing execution and maintained-update
SLA**, not on statutory breadth. What makes it defensible is not that these rules
exist in the product, but that they are **maintained** — through Budget changes,
wage-ceiling revisions, state slab updates, the Form 138 Q4 layout, the ESI cliff,
the Code-era bonus ceilings, and the uneven roll-out of state rules under four Codes.
That maintenance is the operating model, and this spine is its specification.


---

## 07. Functional Requirements — Core HR System of Record

The core HR system of record is the spine that every filing reads from. In a filing-first product this is not a "profile page" module — it is the authoritative, effective-dated source of the exact fields that ECR, ESI challans, PT returns, Form 138 (ex-24Q) and Form 130 (ex-Form 16) are computed and filed against. If a UAN is wrong, the ECR rejects; if a work-location is wrong, PT is remitted to the wrong state; if a date-of-joining is wrong, gratuity accrual and ESI contribution-period membership are wrong. **The system of record is therefore a compliance artefact, not an HR convenience**, and its requirements are written to that standard.

Two design commitments run through every FR below and are stated once here rather than repeated:

- **Everything that feeds a filing is effective-dated and retrospectively recomputable.** This is the same requirement the dual wage base imposes (Code on Wages s.2(y) / Code on Social Security s.2(88), the 50% add-back — see §06) generalised to the whole master. A designation change, a work-location transfer, a bank-account change, a CTC revision — each carries an effective date, and a retro run must recompute against the master *as it stood in the period being corrected*, never as it stands today. **[Verified]** the statutory basis for effective-dating (Source: Code on Wages s.2(y); "or such other per cent as may be notified" makes wage-definition itself a versioned variable).
- **Statutory-impacting fields are maker-checker gated and fully audited.** A change to PAN, UAN, ESI IP number, bank account, Aadhaar, date-of-birth, date-of-joining, PF/ESI eligibility flags or wage components must pass a second-person check and land in an immutable audit log. CERT-In requires 180 days of ICT logs retained *within Indian jurisdiction* with NIC/NPL clock sync (Source: CERT-In Directions, 28.04.2022) — so the audit trail is a regulatory obligation, not a nicety (see §17).

FR identifiers use the prefix `FR-CHR-`. Priority is MoSCoW (**Must** / **Should** / **Could** / **Won't-for-now**); phase maps to the roadmap in §05 (**v1** = files the beachhead, 20–200; **v2** = scales the filing, 200–1,999; **Vision** = enterprise/regulated). Where a MoSCoW "Won't" appears it means *not in the phase named*, with the phase it does land in stated. The employee-lifecycle diagram accompanies §7.3; the entity model accompanies §7.2.

A note on how to read the FR tables: every "Must" in v1 is there because a named filing rejects, a statutory register is incomplete, or a settlement is wrong without it — not because it is expected of an HRMS. Where a field is present only to satisfy a downstream computation, the computation is named. Where a requirement is parity with a free incumbent (Zoho, Frappe, Kredily, Tally) rather than differentiation, it says so, so the roadmap does not over-invest in table stakes (§04 positioning).
