The absolutes are placeholders.** **[Verified — ratio]** / **[Hypothesis — absolutes]**

**Per-task-class token decomposition.** The 23,675/2,045 aggregate hides where the tokens actually go — and where optimisation pays. The decomposition below is an engineering split of the aggregate (**[Hypothesis]**, same kill criterion as the aggregate) and is what §13.9 attribution will replace with measured values:

| Class | Est. share of input tokens | Est. share of output tokens | Scales with | Optimisation lever |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A0 triage | ~5% (1,200) | ~2% (40) | User turns | Tiny prompt; keep on cheapest tier always |
| A1 employee Q&A | ~45% (10,650) | ~35% (715) | Headcount | Rules-first collapses output; read-priced RAG-prefix caching collapses input |
| A2 filing copilot | ~15% (3,550) | ~20% (410) | Admin activity | Structured statutory context; template the explanation |
| A3 bulk docs | ~20% (4,735) | ~30% (615) | Doc volume | Batch API (50% off); template + rules-injected fields |
| A5 analyst copilot | ~10% (2,370) | ~10% (205) | Admin seats | Narrate query results, never compute |
| A4/A6 | ~5% (1,170) | ~3% (60) | Hiring / notifications | A4 metered separately; A6 org-wide fixed |

The read: **A1 and A3 together are ~65% of input and ~65% of output tokens**, and both scale with headcount — they are where cost lives and where rules-first + caching-done-right (§13.4, §13.11) return the most. A0 is negligible per call but high-frequency, so it must *never* leave the cheapest tier. A4/A6 barely move the per-employee number (A4 on its own meter; A6 a fixed org-wide cost amortised across all tenants).

**Batch API economics for async classes (A3, A6).** A3 (bulk documents) and A6 (statutory-change watcher) are latency-tolerant — nobody waits in real time for an appointment-letter run or a notification-classification pass. Both Gemini and Anthropic price a **Batch/async tier at ~50% of standard** (Source: provider batch-pricing pages; **[Hypothesis]** — re-verify; Anthropic's Message Batches API is documented at 50% of standard prices, which anchors the estimate). Routing A3/A6 through the batch tier halves their token cost. Since A3 is ~20–30% of the budget, this is a **~10–15% cut to blended PEPM COGS** for free — the only cost is accepting async (minutes-to-hour) turnaround, which those classes already tolerate. The router must expose a batch-eligible flag per task class and default A3/A6 to it.

**Realistic blended steady-state:** the architecture does not run entirely on one tier. A realistic 2027 blend — A0/A1/A3 on Flash-Lite (2×), A1 escalations + A2/A4/A5/A6 on Flash (2×), frontier at <1% — lands the headcount-scaling PEPM at roughly **₹0.60–₹2.30/employee/month**, matching the §12 range of **₹0.15–3.27**. The low end (₹0.15) assumes aggressive Flash-Lite dominance and Sarvam substitution; the high end (₹3.27) assumes Flash-heavy routing plus a busy analyst copilot.

**Margin envelope against ARPU:**

| ARPU (PEPM, §18 anchor) | AI COGS (steady-state 2027, Flash-heavy ₹2.30) | Gross margin on inference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ₹50 (low, SMB) | ₹2.30 | **95.4%** |
| ₹80 (mid anchor) | ₹2.30 | **97.1%** |
| ₹126 (enterprise-ish) | ₹2.30 | **98.2%** |
| ₹150 (high anchor) | ₹2.30 | **98.5%** |

Even on the pessimistic end (Flash-heavy, post-increase, ₹50 ARPU), inference is **93–99% gross margin** — matching §12. **The COGS mandate holds: bundling AI free never threatens margin at any plausible ARPU.** **[Hypothesis — absolutes pending §20 item V-04]**

**Worked tenant-level examples (steady-state 2027, Rich blend ₹2.30/emp/mo, ₹94.43/USD, before batch discount):**

| Tenant | Headcount | Admins (~1:40) | Monthly AI COGS (headcount classes) | + Analyst copilot (A5, per admin) | Total monthly AI COGS | Tenant monthly ARPU (₹80 PEPM) | COGS % of revenue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Small SMB | 25 | 1 | ₹57.50 | ~₹15 | ~₹72 | ₹2,000 | 3.6% |
| Beachhead mid | 100 | 2–3 | ₹230 | ~₹40 | ~₹270 | ₹8,000 | 3.4% |
| Beachhead top | 200 | 4–5 | ₹460 | ~₹75 | ~₹535 | ₹16,000 | 3.3% |

(A5 estimated as a per-admin analyst load; **[Hypothesis]** — instrument in §20 item V-04.) The pattern holds across the band: **AI COGS sits at ~3–4% of revenue regardless of tenant size**, because both the numerator (headcount-scaling tokens) and denominator (per-seat ARPU) scale with headcount. Applying the A3/A6 batch discount (§13.6) and a Lean routing bias pulls this toward ~1.5–2%. This size-invariance is *why* free bundling is safe across the entire 20–200 beachhead.

**Latency and SLA tiering — a cost input, not just UX.** Task classes split cleanly by latency tolerance, and latency tolerance is a cost lever (batch pricing) and a routing input:

| Latency tier | Classes | Tolerance | Cost implication |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Real-time (<2s) | A0, A1 | Employee is waiting | Cheapest fast tier; rules-first keeps output tiny so time-to-answer is short |
| Interactive (<10s) | A2, A5 | Admin is working | Mid tier; occasional escalation acceptable |
| Async (minutes–1h) | A3, A4, A6 | Nobody waiting | **Batch tier (50% off)** — the latency tolerance *is* the discount |

The design rule: **never pay real-time pricing for an async class.** A3/A4/A6 default to batch; only A0/A1/A2/A5 justify synchronous pricing. This is the same insight as §13.6's batch lever, stated as a routing default.

The stress test that matters: **at what point does bundling AI free break the low end?** Solving for AI COGS = 10% of a ₹50 ARPU seat = ₹5.00/employee/month. That is **~2.2× the pessimistic Flash-heavy steady-state**, i.e. actual tokens would have to come in at 2.2× the engineering estimate *and* stay Flash-heavy *and* run at ₹50 ARPU simultaneously. §20 item V-04's kill criterion (actual 5× estimate) is the real breakpoint; at 5× estimate, low-end bundling economics invert and metered SKUs (§13.8) must carry more.

### 13.7 Rate limits, budgets and graceful degradation — the per-user blowout

 **[Verified]** — **Per-tenant and per-user rate limits are P0.** An HRMS is priced *per employee* but consumed *per user*. One heavy user can exceed the entire ARPU for that seat. Even Microsoft hard-disables agents at 125% of prepaid capacity (§12). (Source: §12, Microsoft Copilot capacity policy.)

The PEPM-vs-per-user mismatch is the single most dangerous cost dynamic in the model, and it is invisible in the blended PEPM figure. A 50-person tenant pays for 50 seats of ARPU but might have three power users (an HR admin running the analyst copilot all day, a manager bulk-drafting offer letters, an employee stuck in a Q&A loop) who between them consume 40% of the tenant's tokens. Without limits, those three users can push a single tenant's AI COGS past its entire ARPU.

**Worked blowout.** A single admin runs the A5 analyst copilot in a tight loop — "show me attrition by department", "now by location", "now overlay tenure", 200 queries in a day, a few escalating to frontier. At frontier's ₹16/1000-token-workload equivalent, even 10 frontier escalations is ~₹160 for one admin in one day — more than a ₹150-ARPU seat's *monthly* revenue. The per-user budget is what stops one curious admin from erasing a tenant's margin, and the frontier rate-limit (§13.5, §13.16 item 10) is what stops the escalations specifically.

**Worked edge case — A5 multi-turn context growth (the compounding input-token leak).** The analyst copilot is conversational: "attrition by department" → "now by location" → "now only for tenure < 1 year". If the full conversation history plus the growing result set is resent as context on every turn, input tokens compound turn-over-turn — turn 10 can carry 10× the context of turn 1, and A5 is a *mid*-tier (Flash) class, so this is real money. Two controls: (a) narrate results, never carry raw result rows into context — the model needs the *shape* of the answer, not every row (the query engine holds the data, the model describes it); (b) bound conversation context with a sliding window or summary so an all-day analyst session does not accumulate an unbounded prefix. This is the A5 analogue of A1's retrieval-bloat problem (§13.4): in both, input tokens leak through context the *product* prepends, not through anything the user typed, and both are invisible until per-tenant attribution (§13.9) surfaces an A5 input-token line growing with session length rather than query count.

**Graceful degradation is a defined state machine, not an error path.** "Degrade gracefully" must be specified, or it degrades into "throw an error." The states, in order of preference on any budget/health/post-check failure:

| Trigger | Degraded behaviour | User sees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Post-check mismatch (§13.4) | Drop generated wrapper, return templated engine values | Correct figure, plainer prose |
| Per-user soft budget breach | Continue but log; optionally add a one-line "usage is high" note | No change to answer |
| Per-user hard budget breach | Rules-only templated answer for A1/A2; queue for A3; soft-block A5 | Correct figure or "queued", never "broken" |
| All in-tier backends unhealthy (§13.5) | Rules-only templated answer | Correct figure, plainer prose |
| Terminal low-confidence after capped escalation | Rules-only answer + flag for human review | Correct figure + "an admin will confirm" |

The through-line: **the answer (the statutory figure) always survives degradation, because it never came from the model.** Only the fluent wrapper is at risk, and dropping it is a UX downgrade, never a correctness or availability failure. This is only possible *because* of rules-first (§13.4) — a product that let the model compute figures would have no safe degraded state.

**Required controls (P0):**

- **Per-user token budget**, refreshed per period, with soft/hard thresholds. Soft threshold logs and (optionally) throttles; hard threshold degrades gracefully — fall back to a rules-only / templated response, or queue the request, never a hard error that reads as "the product is broken".
- **Per-tenant token budget** as a backstop, sized as a multiple of tenant ARPU (e.g. hard cap at ~15–20% of tenant ARPU spent on tokens, well above the ~2% steady-state, so it only ever catches abuse or a bug).
- **Meter, budget, degrade — in that order.** Graceful degradation for A1/A2 means "answer from the deterministic rules layer and skip the generated wrapper" — the *answer* (the PF figure) is still correct because it never came from the model; only the prose wrapper is dropped. The templated fallback is the *same* mechanism as the post-check fallback (§13.4): one code path, three triggers (post-check mismatch, budget exhaustion, provider outage).
- **Spike-aware, not just abuse-aware.** The budget must survive the legitimate payday and Form-130 spikes (§13.3) — a per-user monthly budget sized for average load will throttle honest employees on exactly the days they most need an answer. Size per-user budgets against *peak-day* load, and let the per-tenant backstop, not the per-user throttle, catch genuine abuse.
- **Recruiting metered separately** (next section) — its cost driver is hiring velocity, not headcount, so it must never draw from the per-employee budget.

 **[Verified]** — **Recruiting cost does not track headcount.** A tenant hiring at 15%/month against one hiring at 3%/month is a **15× cost difference on identical PEPM pricing.** greytHR already concedes the pattern by pricing Recruit per recruiter, not per employee (§18). (Source: §18, greytHR Recruit pricing.) A4 must be budgeted and (if monetised) priced against requisitions/hires, on its own meter, isolated from the per-employee envelope.

### 13.8 Metered surfaces — where AI spend is allowed to become price

§18 names the only three places where the unit of value is legibly incremental and AI spend may be recovered as price. Pricing them here means recovering *incremental cost* on a cost driver that does not track headcount — not charging a margin on intelligence (which the zero anchor forbids).

| Surface | Cost driver | Meter | Pricing logic | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Recruiting (A4)** | Hiring velocity | Per requisition or per hire | Recover A4 token cost + a thin margin on the *sourcing/screening* value, not on headcount | greytHR precedent: Recruit priced per recruiter, not per employee. Never blend into PEPM. |
| **Bulk document generation (A3 at volume)** | Document volume spikes (onboarding waves, appraisal-letter runs) | Per document above a bundled quota | Base plan includes a monthly quota; overage priced per doc | Quota sized so normal churn is free; only bulk events (mass onboarding) meter |
| **HR-analyst copilot (A5)** | Admin analyst usage | Per admin seat | Priced per *analyst admin seat*, not per employee | This is where occasional frontier escalation lives — its cost is recovered by the per-seat price |

**Worked recovery example (recruiting).** Suppose one requisition consumes ~30k input / 5k output tokens across JD generation, 40 resume parses, and screening summaries. At Flash (post-2×, ₹94.43): ~₹4.20 in inference. A per-requisition price of even ₹200–500 (a rounding error against the ₹5,000–15,000 a bureau or agency charges to fill a role) recovers inference **50–100× over** and leaves the incremental-value margin §18 permits — without ever charging a "margin on intelligence." The point is not that recruiting AI is expensive; it is that its cost driver (hiring velocity) is *legibly separable* from headcount, so a per-requisition price is defensible where a per-employee AI surcharge is not.

**Rule:** these three prices recover a cost that is *legibly incremental and does not track headcount*. They are not an "AI premium" — a premium reads as a surcharge on an expected feature and dies against the zero anchor (§18, §20 non-goal "Premium AI SKU"). A per-requisition recruiting price is defensible because *hiring is a discrete, budgeted event*; a per-admin-seat analyst price is defensible because *analysts are a countable, provisioned role*. The base assistant (A0/A1/A2) stays free forever.

 **[Hypothesis — validation: §20 item V-07, Van Westendorp/conjoint, 30–40 buyers]** — willingness to pay for any HR-AI SKU is unvalidated. If §20 item V-07 reports genuine zero willingness everywhere, **drop the metered AI SKUs entirely** and treat A4/A5 purely as COGS to be minimised. The architecture must not depend on metered-AI revenue; it is upside, not thesis. This is also why A4/A5 must be attributed separately from v1 (§13.9): if the SKUs are dropped, we still need to know their COGS to decide whether to keep, cap, or cut the feature.

### 13.9 Cost attribution — build it while the price is zero

 **[Verified]** — **Build full token, cache and cost attribution per tenant, user, agent and model from v1, while the price is still zero.** Retrofitting attribution after pricing exists is far harder than building it before (§18). (Source: §18 architecture requirement.)

Attribution is the instrument that makes every other decision in this section measurable. Without it, the ₹0.15–3.27 figures stay forever [Hypothesis]; with it, §20 item V-04 closes and the model moves to [Verified].

**Attribution record (emitted per routed call, P0 schema):**

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `tenant_id` | Per-tenant COGS, tenant-level margin, abuse detection |
| `user_id` | Per-user rate limiting, power-user detection |
| `agent / task_class` | Which of A0–A6 spent the tokens; where to optimise |
| `model / provider` | Actual model used (post-routing), for the tier→model attribution |
| `model_list_price_ref` | The list price the model was priced against, so COGS reconstructs even after a provider re-prices (§13.5) |
| `input_tokens / output_tokens / cache_read / cache_write` | The raw cost inputs |
| `escalated` (bool) + reason | Escalation-rate monitoring (a rising rate is a margin leak) |
| `fx_rate_at_call` | So historical COGS is reconstructable at the rate in force (§13.2) |
| `residency_region` | Per-tenant residency compliance audit (§13.10) |
| `rules_fallback` (bool) + reason | Whether graceful degradation fired, and why (post-check / budget / outage) — §13.7 |

**Derived metrics this unlocks (all P0 dashboards):**

- **PEPM COGS per tenant** — the real number that replaces the §12 [Hypothesis] band.
- **COGS as % of ARPU per tenant** — the margin-erosion early-warning; any tenant above ~5% is investigated.
- **Escalation rate per task class** — Flash-Lite→Flash escalations; a leading indicator of prompt/retrieval quality problems.
- **Cache economics per tenant** (see §13.11) — because caching inverts by tenant size.
- **Frontier-call rate** — must stay <1%; each frontier call is ~50× a cheapest call.
- **Rules-fallback rate per task class** — a rising A1/A2 fallback rate means the *generation* layer is failing the post-check often (a quality problem), even though the *answer* stays correct; this is invisible to the customer but visible in COGS/quality terms only via attribution.

**Attribution logs are themselves a residency and CERT-In obligation.** The attribution stream contains `tenant_id`, `user_id`, and enough context to link a query to an employee — it is employee-related ICT data. CERT-In requires **180 days of ICT logs retained within Indian jurisdiction** and 6-hour incident reporting, and names attacks on AI/ML systems as a reportable incident class (item xx of twenty) (§17). So the attribution store is not free-floating telemetry: it must be India-resident for regulated tenants, retained ≥180 days, and clock-synced to NIC/NPL NTP so timestamps are admissible. Build this into the schema and storage location from v1 — retrofitting log residency after the fact is exactly the kind of painful migration §17 warns about. **[Verified — CERT-In directions, §17]**

The discipline point from §18: attribution is *cheapest to build before pricing exists*, because there is no billing system arguing with it yet and no customer disputing a line item. Build it in month zero.

### 13.10 Provider abstraction, residency, and the INR-native hedge

Provider abstraction serves cost (§13.5), FX (§13.2), and residency simultaneously. Residency is the constraint that makes ≥3 interchangeable backends a hard requirement rather than a cost optimisation.

 **[Verified]** — **Residency is a per-provider matrix, and data-at-rest residency is a different guarantee from in-country inference — buyers ask about both** (§17). OpenAI offers India data-at-rest plus Bedrock for in-country inference; Anthropic offers neither, with a US-only immutable workspace geo; Vertex has an India region. Sarvam's hosting is **unverified and must not be relied on until it is.** (Source: provider residency documentation captured in §17.)

**Provider residency matrix (as captured in §17; re-verify before any regulated-tenant commit):**

| Provider | India data-at-rest | In-country inference | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI | Yes | Yes (via Bedrock) | **[Verified]** |
| Anthropic | No | No (US-only immutable workspace geo) | **[Verified]** |
| Google Vertex (Gemini) | India region exists | India region exists | **[Verified]** |
| Sarvam | Claimed INR-native, India-hosted | Claimed | **[Hypothesis — unverified; do not rely until confirmed. Kill criterion: if Sarvam cannot contractually guarantee India residency, it cannot serve regulated tenants and its role narrows to a cost/FX hedge for non-regulated tenants only]** |

**The residency consequence for the router (worked).** The frontier tier is Claude Opus 4.8, which per the matrix has **no India data-at-rest and no in-country inference**. Therefore for a regulated tenant (bank, insurer), the frontier escalation tier must be **disabled outright** — there is no India-resident frontier available, so an A5 query that would escalate simply degrades to the best India-resident mid tier and, if needed, flags for human review. This is not a cost decision; it is a hard compliance gate, and it is why the router carries the residency flag *before* it consults the cost/tier map (§13.16 item 4). A non-regulated 30-person tenant, by contrast, routes on cheapest-global with frontier available.

**The two roles of the INR-native provider (Sarvam):**

1. **FX hedge.** When USD/INR breaches ₹100 (§20 risk trigger), the router shifts USD-priced classes onto INR-denominated Sarvam for classes where quality permits (A0/A1/A3 first — the cheapest, highest-volume, lowest-risk). An INR-priced provider is structurally immune to the depreciation that erodes every USD-priced tier.
2. **Residency answer for regulated tenants** — *only if* its India hosting is verified. Until then, its residency role is **zero** and it is a cost/FX play only.

 **[Verified]** — **AI architecture is foreclosed by regulation for regulated buyers, and the decision cannot be deferred** (§17). RBI's Outsourcing of IT Services Directions impose data localisation, right-to-audit (including by RBI), sub-contracting consent and exit obligations on any SaaS vendor serving a regulated entity — **with no turnover threshold.** SBI's RFP requires all data functions and processing within India; IRDAI mandates records in Indian data centres. (Source: RBI Outsourcing of IT Services Directions; SBI HRMS RFP; IRDAI records regulations, all per §17.)

**Requirement (carried from §12):** at least three interchangeable backends with **residency selectable per tenant.** A regulated tenant is pinned to an India-region provider (Vertex India, or verified-Sarvam) for *every* task class, with the frontier escalation tier *disabled* for that tenant if no India-resident frontier exists. A non-regulated 30-person tenant runs on the cheapest global routing. **The router carries the residency flag per tenant and enforces it before cost routing.** This is the same abstraction serving two constraints — one piece of work.

**The sub-contracting-consent trap (worked).** RBI's directions require the regulated entity's consent for sub-contracting and impose an exit obligation. In router terms: a regulated tenant's *set of permitted providers* is contractually fixed and cannot silently change. So the "re-point without deploy" capability (§13.5) — which is a pure win for cost management on non-regulated tenants — must be *constrained* for regulated tenants: re-pointing a regulated tenant's class to a new provider is a contractual event (consent + right-to-audit of the new sub-processor), not a config edit. The router config must therefore distinguish "freely re-pointable" (non-regulated) from "consent-gated" (regulated) tier maps. This is a design requirement, not a runtime one, but it must be in the schema from v1.

**DPDP tailwind (from §17):** DPDP s.7(i) — employers do not need employee consent to process employee data for employment purposes. This removes the consent-UX friction that GDPR-bound AI-HR products carry, a genuine structural advantage for building AI-first in India. **[Verified]** (Source: DPDP Act s.7(i), §17.) But it does *not* remove the residency obligation for regulated buyers, nor the CERT-In log obligations (§13.9) — those are independent constraints. DPDP frees us from a *consent* burden; it does nothing about a *localisation* burden.

**Self-host is not a cost play.** **[Verified — §12/§20]** Serverless beats dedicated H100 by ~74× at realistic utilisation. Self-hosting inference "to save money" is a non-goal. Self-host exists *only* as a priced compliance SKU for named regulated accounts that contractually require it — its cost is recovered from that account, never absorbed into the base COGS model. (Source: §12 utilisation analysis; §20 non-goal.)

### 13.11 Caching — a per-tenant, per-provider policy, never a default

 **[Killed]** — **"Cache everything" would have caused real damage.** Caching economics *invert* by provider and tenant size. Gemini charges *hourly cache storage*; a 50k-token per-tenant policy cache held continuously on Flash-Lite costs roughly **₹34.47 per employee at a 100-employee tenant, against ₹0.27 for simply paying full input price** — about **100× that tenant's entire inference bill** (§12). (Source: Gemini cache-storage pricing, §12.)

This is the most counter-intuitive cost result in the model and the one most likely to be re-introduced by a well-meaning engineer, so it is stated as a hard rule:

- **Caching is a per-provider, per-tenant-size policy decision, never a default.** The reflexive "cache the policy corpus" move is correct on providers that price cache by *read* and catastrophic on providers (Gemini) that price cache by *storage-hour*.
- **The break-even is tenant-size-dependent.** A large tenant with high query volume amortises a held cache; a 100-employee tenant querying occasionally pays 100× to hold a cache it barely reads. Attribution (§13.9) must track cache economics *per tenant* so the router's cache policy can be set per tenant-size band.
- **Prefer stateless full-input pricing for small tenants.** For the beachhead (20–200 employees), the default is *no held cache* — pay full input price per call, which the token budget already assumes. Held caching is opted into only for large tenants where the read volume amortises the storage-hour cost, and only on providers where that math works.
- **Prompt-prefix / ephemeral caching (read-priced) is different and generally fine** — where a provider prices cache reads at ~0.1× input and does not charge storage-hours, caching a stable system-prompt prefix or policy-corpus prefix is a straightforward win, and it is the primary lever against the RAG-retrieval bloat in §13.4. The [Killed] finding is specifically about *held, storage-hour-priced* caches on Gemini for small tenants. Distinguish the two in the router config; do not let the [Killed] finding suppress the legitimate read-priced win.

**Worked break-even.** Held cache on Gemini Flash-Lite, 50k tokens, storage-hour priced: cost is fixed per hour regardless of reads. For a 100-employee tenant issuing ~450 A1 queries/month (§13.3), that is <1 read per hour on average — the held cache is idle 99% of the time it is billed. Full-input pricing, by contrast, is paid *only when a query runs*. The held cache only wins once read frequency is high enough that the amortised storage-hour cost per read drops below the full-input price per read — which happens at large-tenant / high-query-density scale, not at the beachhead. Set the policy per (provider × tenant-size-band), default **off** below ~1,000 employees, and let attribution move the threshold as real read densities come in.

**The legitimate win, quantified.** Read-priced prefix caching (cache reads at ~0.1× input, no storage-hour charge) is the *opposite* economics and is worth taking. A1's input is dominated by the stable prefix: the system prompt + the tenant's policy-corpus chunks that recur across many employees' questions (§13.4). If that prefix is ~3,000 tokens of the ~10,650 A1 input tokens/emp/mo, and it is cached at ~0.1× read cost across the ~450 A1 calls/mo that share it, the prefix's input cost falls roughly 90% — a **~25–30% cut to A1 input cost** with no held-cache storage risk, on providers that price this way. This is why the [Killed] finding must be scoped precisely: kill *held, storage-hour-priced* caches for small tenants, keep *read-priced prefix* caches everywhere the provider supports them. Attribution (§13.9) tracks `cache_read`/`cache_write` per tenant precisely so this distinction is measured, not assumed.

**Design rule:** the cache policy is a router config field per (provider × tenant-size-band), instrumented by §13.9, defaulting to **off** for held caches on the beachhead and **on** for read-priced prefix caching where the provider supports it. It is never a global "cache everything" default. **[Killed — global cache-everything default; §20 non-goal "Cache-everything default"]**

### 13.12 FX sensitivity — the full model at ₹90 / ₹95 / ₹100

FX is modelled at three levels per the risk register. The table below shows steady-state 2027 (post-Flash-increase) blended AI COGS per employee-month, and the ₹100 row is the trigger point for the Sarvam shift (§13.10).

**Assumptions:** blended workload on the 23,675/2,045 budget; realistic 2027 routing (mostly Flash-Lite for A0/A1/A3, Flash for A2/A4/A5/A6, <1% frontier); post-Jan-2027 Flash pricing (2×). Two blend scenarios: **Lean** (Flash-Lite-dominant, aggressive routing) and **Rich** (Flash-heavy, busy analyst copilot).

| USD/INR | Lean blend (₹/emp/mo) | Rich blend (₹/emp/mo) | COGS as % of ₹80 ARPU (Rich) | Router action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **₹90** | ₹0.57 | ₹2.20 | 2.8% | Steady state, USD routing |
| **₹95** | ₹0.60 | ₹2.32 | 2.9% | Steady state, USD routing |
| **₹100** | ₹0.63 | ₹2.45 | 3.1% | **Trigger: shift A0/A1/A3 to Sarvam (INR-native), holds COGS flat vs further depreciation** |

(All figures **[Hypothesis]** on absolutes, **[Verified]** on the FX proportionality — cost scales linearly with the rupee for USD-priced tiers.)

**The load-bearing observations from this table:**

- **FX moves COGS by ~11% across the ₹90→₹100 range** (linear in the rupee for USD-priced tiers). At 93–99% margins, an 11% swing in a 2–3%-of-ARPU cost is immaterial to the business case. **FX is a real strategic input but not a margin threat** — the router's Sarvam shift caps the downside.
- **The Sarvam shift at ₹100 is a hedge, not a rescue.** Even without it, ₹100/USD leaves COGS at ~3% of ARPU. The shift matters more if the rupee runs *past* ₹100, or if actual tokens come in above the estimate (§20 item V-04) — that is when INR-native routing changes the margin picture materially.
- **The Sarvam shift is only available for non-regulated tenants until residency is verified.** Note the interaction with §13.10: the ₹100 FX trigger says "shift A0/A1/A3 to Sarvam", but a regulated tenant may already be pinned to Vertex India for residency, and cannot move to an unverified-residency provider regardless of FX. So the FX hedge and the residency pin can conflict — the residency pin always wins. For regulated tenants, the FX hedge is Vertex India (INR-billed if available) or simply absorbing the depreciation, not Sarvam.
- **The combined shock (₹100 + Flash 2× + 5× token estimate) is the real stress case.** ₹2.45 × (5×/current-blend-multiplier) pushes Rich-blend COGS toward ₹8–10/employee/month = 10–20% of a ₹50 ARPU seat. *That* is where low-end free-bundling breaks and metered SKUs (§13.8) must carry the load. It requires all three adverse conditions at once; the router (FX shift) and rules-first (token suppression) are the two levers that keep it off.



**Figure 86. Fx Sensitivity**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    base["FX baseline: USD/INR ₹94.43 (Sep 2026)<br/>Steady-state 2027 = post-Flash-2x<br/>Budget 23,675 in / 2,045 out tokens/emp/mo<br/>USD-priced tiers scale linearly with the rupee"]

    base --> fx90 & fx95 & fx100

    subgraph model["FX sensitivity — blended AI COGS per employee-month"]
        direction TB
        fx90["USD/INR ₹90<br/>Lean ₹0.57 · Rich ₹2.20<br/>2.8% of ₹80 ARPU<br/>Steady state, USD routing"]
        fx95["USD/INR ₹95<br/>Lean ₹0.60 · Rich ₹2.32<br/>2.9% of ₹80 ARPU<br/>Steady state, USD routing"]
        fx100["USD/INR ₹100 (risk-register trigger)<br/>Lean ₹0.63 · Rich ₹2.45<br/>3.1% of ₹80 ARPU"]
    end

    fx90 -. "~11% COGS swing ₹90 to ₹100<br/>immaterial at 93-99% margin" .-> fx100

    fx100 --> trigger{"Router action at ₹100:<br/>shift A0/A1/A3 to<br/>Sarvam (INR-native)?"}

    trigger --> nonreg["Non-regulated tenant:<br/>shift to Sarvam<br/>caps COGS vs further depreciation<br/>(hedge, not rescue — ₹100 alone still ~3%)"]
    trigger --> reg["Regulated tenant:<br/>residency pin WINS over FX hedge<br/>stay on Vertex India (INR-billed)<br/>or absorb depreciation<br/>Sarvam residency unverified"]

    stress --> breaks["Low-end free bundling breaks<br/>metered SKUs (§13.8) must carry load<br/>needs all 3 adverse conditions at once"]

    nonreg --> hedged["FX capped: router (FX shift)<br/>+ rules-first (token suppression)<br/>keep the stress case off"]
    reg --> hedged
```


### 13.13 The statutory-change watcher (A6) — an org-wide fixed cost, amortised

A6 is the one class whose cost does **not** scale with tenants at all — it is a single org-wide pipeline that ingests EPFO, ESIC, CBDT, and state-labour notifications, classifies each as *amendment vs new instrument* (§12: "catch amendments, not just new instruments" — a watcher keyed only to new notifications would have missed the corrigendum that inverted the entire November 2026 EPF analysis), and drafts a change summary for the statutory team. It is human-in-loop by design; its output is never auto-applied to any tenant's rules.

Because it runs once for the whole company, not once per tenant, its per-employee cost is a *rounding error that shrinks as the customer base grows*:

| Notification volume | Est. tokens/notification (ingest + classify + draft) | Monthly A6 token cost (batch tier) | Amortised across 1,000 tenants / 100k employees |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ~200 notifications/month (all sources, incl. state) | ~15,000 in / ~2,000 out | ~₹15–30/month total | **< ₹0.0003/employee/month** |

(All **[Hypothesis]** — notification volume from the four Labour Codes' uneven state roll-out (§06) is itself unmeasured; instrument once live.) The point stands regardless of the exact figure: **A6 is org-wide fixed, batch-priced, and amortises to effectively zero per employee.** The expensive part of the statutory-change operating model is *not* the tokens — it is the permanent human statutory team (§01's "compliance-maintenance operation, not a feature-velocity startup"). A6's job is to make that team's scarce attention 10× more leveraged by pre-filtering and pre-drafting, not to replace it. The COGS of A6 is negligible; the *value* is that a ₹30/month pipeline surfaces the one corrigendum that would otherwise cost a wrong-filing liability across every tenant.

**Design requirement — the corrigendum classifier is the whole point.** A6 must classify amendment-vs-new and flag *superseding corrigenda specifically*, because the November 2026 failure mode (§06) was a corrigendum (S.O. 5319(E) enumeration, later corrected) that amended an earlier notification — a watcher that only alerts on new instruments reproduces the exact round-one error. Two concrete build rules follow: (1) the watcher must monitor the *gazette*, not only indiacode.nic.in, because indiacode's bare-Act footnote still reproduces the uncorrected enumeration (§06) — an A6 keyed to indiacode alone would ingest the *wrong* text; (2) any A6 output that touches a live rule (EPF 12%, ESI rates, a PT slab) must carry a "check-for-corrigendum" flag that the human statutory team clears before the rules engine is updated (§13.4's effective-dated, versioned change). The model drafts; the statutory team decides; the rules engine is updated by a human. This is the AI cost layer's contribution to the PRD's standing rule (front matter): *"Check for a corrigendum" is non-negotiable.* **[Verified — §06 November 2026 corrigendum failure mode]**

**The unresolved-ESI edge case (a v1 correctness dependency A6 must watch).** §06 flags that the ESI regime post-22 November 2026 is *unresolved* — the one-year saving of ESI rules under CoSS s.164(2)(b) expires and there is no named successor scheme (unlike EPF's Scheme 2026). This is a §20 item V-08 open question with a hard date. A6 is the mechanism that must catch the ESIC/MoLE notification the moment it lands, because ESI rates (0.75%/3.25%) are exactly the kind of deterministic figure the rules engine owns (§13.4) and cannot compute correctly if the underlying scheme changes silently. A6's ESI watch is therefore not optional monitoring — it is a payroll-engine-correctness dependency with a countdown.

### 13.14 What COGS discipline buys against the competitive set

The zero anchor (§18) is usually read as a threat — we cannot charge for AI. Reframed through the cost model, **COGS discipline is a structural advantage against exactly the vendors who set the price to zero.**

Every vendor in the §18 table gives AI away. The question is who can *afford* to. The answer depends entirely on their inference COGS discipline — which is invisible in their pricing but decisive in their margins:

- **A vendor bundling a frontier-tier assistant free** (no rules-first, no router, cache-everything) could be running AI COGS of **₹16+/employee/month** (our frontier row) — 5–50× ours. At ₹50–150 ARPU that is a 10–30% margin hit they are absorbing to match the zero anchor. That is survivable for a Zoho or a Microsoft with cross-subsidy; it is fatal for a pure-play HRMS with 137%-of-revenue staff costs (Keka, §04) or a 0.8% EBITDA margin (ZingHR). (Source: filed revenue figures, §04. **[Verified]** on the competitor financials; **[Hypothesis]** on their inference COGS.)
- **Our discipline (rules-first + router + batch + attribution) targets ₹0.60–2.30/employee/month.** We can match the zero anchor *and* keep 93–99% inference margin. The zero price costs our competitors margin; it costs us almost nothing.

**Worked margin comparison (illustrative, ₹80 ARPU, per employee-month).** The point is not the exact figures — it is the *ratio* of margin impact between a disciplined and an undisciplined operator matching the same zero price:

| Operator posture | AI COGS/emp/mo | Inference margin at ₹80 ARPU | Margin *given up* to match zero anchor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Us (rules-first + router + batch) | ₹0.60–2.30 | 97–99% | ~1–3% of ARPU |
| Naive Flash-heavy, no rules-first | ₹8–12 | 85–90% | ~10–15% of ARPU |
| Frontier-bundled, cache-everything | ₹16+ | ≤80% | ≥20% of ARPU |

(All rows except our own are **[Hypothesis]** — competitor COGS is unobservable; the naive/frontier rows are our own cost model run *without* the discipline levers, as a proxy for what an undisciplined competitor would spend.) A vendor giving up 20% of ARPU to bundle AI free is fine if they cross-subsidise (Zoho, Microsoft) and fatal if they don't (a pure-play at 137%-of-revenue staff cost). We give up ~1–3%. **Same free price, wildly different survivability.**

**The strategic read:** the zero anchor is a moat *for the disciplined operator*. It forces every entrant to give AI away, and only the entrant whose COGS is a rounding error can do that indefinitely without cross-subsidy. Our cost architecture is not a defensive necessity — it is the thing that makes "AI-native, price-on-filing" survivable where a naive AI-first competitor bleeds margin matching a price they cannot afford. **[Hypothesis — depends on competitor COGS being undisciplined; unobservable directly, inferred from their frontier-model marketing. Kill/validate: if a competitor's public technical material reveals rules-first + routing discipline comparable to ours, this advantage narrows. Do not put in a deck as fact.]**

This also sharpens the §20 non-goal "Premium AI SKU": a surcharge on AI is not just unsellable against the zero anchor — it would *signal* to competitors that our COGS is high enough to need recovery. Bundling free while running near-zero COGS is both the sellable posture and the one that reveals nothing about our cost structure.

### 13.15 The MCP / assistant-convergence risk to the cost thesis

 **[Killed / caution — §20]** — There is *no evidence* that shipping an MCP server has changed a single buying decision; MCP adoption statistics from round one are banned (§20). Darwinbox already ships Cortex into Teams, Copilot, Slack and Glean. (Source: §12; §20 banned-figures list.)

The cost-model consequence: **if enterprise buyers converge on Copilot/Glean as the assistant, our AI COGS *drops toward zero* for those tenants** — the buyer's assistant calls our MCP tools, and *they* pay for the inference. This is not a threat to the cost model; it is a tail-wind on COGS and a threat to *differentiation* (which collapses to data quality and tool design — §12.7's "own the data and the tools, not the assistant" posture). Three implications:

- **The cost model must not assume every tenant runs our assistant.** A meaningful fraction of enterprise tenants may route their AI through their own Copilot seats. Model AI COGS as *declining* with enterprise mix, not rising.
- **The metered surfaces (§13.8) are more exposed than the base assistant.** If the buyer's Copilot can call our recruiting/analyst tools directly, the per-seat/per-requisition price is harder to defend. This reinforces §18: monetise the *data and tools*, and treat metered-AI revenue as upside that may erode as assistant-convergence proceeds.
- **The rules-first guardrail (§13.4) must hold even when the assistant is someone else's.** If a buyer's Copilot calls our MCP tools, *their* model generates the prose — we do not control its prompt or its post-check. So the MCP tool must return the statutory figure as a **structured, typed field the caller cannot easily corrupt into prose**, and the tool contract must make clear the figure is authoritative and not to be recomputed. Our correctness guarantee cannot depend on a model we do not run; it must live in the tool's response contract. This is the assistant-convergence version of the §13.4 mandate, and it is why "own the tools, not the assistant" is a correctness posture, not only a differentiation one.

### 13.16 Acceptance criteria for the AI cost layer

The AI economics layer is "done for v1" when all of the following hold. These are testable, not aspirational.

| # | Acceptance criterion | Verifies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | No monetary/statutory figure in any AI output originates from the model; a deterministic post-check rejects any output whose monetary/percentage/date tokens do not match an engine-supplied value, and the fallback returns the raw engine values in a template | §13.4 rules-first |
| 2 | Task class → tier → model is a hot-reloadable config table; re-pointing a class requires no deploy; regulated-tenant tier maps are marked consent-gated and cannot be silently re-pointed | §13.5, §13.10 router |
| 3 | ≥3 interchangeable backends configured; failover on backend outage is automatic; escalation depth is capped (no unbounded Lite→Flash→frontier loop) | §13.5 |
| 4 | Residency is a per-tenant flag enforced *before* cost routing; a regulated-tenant test case never routes to a non-India-resident provider, and the frontier tier is disabled for a regulated tenant with no India-resident frontier | §13.10 |
| 5 | Per-user and per-tenant token budgets with soft/hard thresholds; hard-threshold breach degrades to rules-only response, never a hard error; per-user budgets sized against peak-day (payday/Form-130) load | §13.7 |
| 6 | Recruiting (A4) metered on its own budget, isolated from the per-employee envelope; A4/A5 attributed separately so their COGS is known even if the metered SKU is dropped | §13.7, §13.8 |
| 7 | Full attribution record (§13.9 schema) emitted per call from v1; per-tenant PEPM-COGS and COGS-%-of-ARPU dashboards live; attribution store is India-resident and ≥180-day-retained for regulated tenants (CERT-In) | §13.9 |
| 8 | Cache policy is per-(provider × tenant-size-band) config, defaulting to OFF for the beachhead; no global cache-everything path exists; read-priced prefix caching is available as a distinct, allowed config | §13.11 |
| 9 | FX rate is a runtime input recorded per call; cost model recomputes at ₹90/95/100; ₹100 trigger shifts configured non-regulated classes to INR-native routing | §13.2, §13.12 |
| 10 | Frontier-tier calls are rate-limited hard and monitored; frontier-call rate <1% of all calls; frontier disabled entirely for regulated tenants | §13.5, §13.6, §13.10 |
| 11 | A6 statutory watcher classifies amendment-vs-new, flags superseding corrigenda, monitors the gazette (not only indiacode), and its output is human-cleared before any rules-engine update | §13.13 |
| 12 | MCP tools return statutory figures as typed authoritative fields (not free prose), so the rules-first guarantee holds when the caller's assistant generates the wrapper | §13.15 |

### 13.17 Instrumenting the one number that matters — the §20 item V-04 plan

Every absolute rupee figure in this section is downstream of one measurement: **actual tokens per employee-month against a real policy corpus and real query mix.** §20 item V-04 names it as the gate on all absolute AI cost figures. This subsection specifies *how* to close it, because "instrument a prototype" is not a plan until it is.

**What must be measured, and against what.** The engineering estimate (23,675 in / 2,045 out) is an aggregate. The instrumentation must produce a *per-task-class* breakdown (the §13.6 decomposition table, with measured values replacing the estimates) plus the two other unmeasured drivers: the A1 query rate (~6 turns/emp/mo, §13.3) and the RAG retrieval size per A1 call (§13.4). Measure against a *representative* corpus, not a toy one: a real 100–200-page tenant policy set (leave, conduct, POSH, travel, the statutory FAQ), because A1 input tokens are dominated by retrieved policy chunks, and corpus size is the variable that most breaks the estimate.

**Methodology (before any price commit):**

1. **Stand up the router + attribution (§13.5, §13.9) in a prototype**, not a spreadsheet. The attribution schema *is* the measurement instrument — every routed call already emits `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `task_class`, `cache_read/write`. Instrumenting is therefore not extra work; it is the P0 attribution layer run against a realistic load.
2. **Replay a realistic query mix.** Seed A1 with the real questions employees ask (payroll: "why is my PF/TDS lower", leave balance, policy lookups), A2 with real filing-reconciliation asks, A5 with real analyst queries. Source the query list from the CA/bureau interviews (§20 items V-01, V-05) and any early design-partner tenant — do not invent the mix.
3. **Measure per employee-month, per class, at realistic query rate.** Run enough employee-months of simulated load to get a stable per-class token distribution (not just a mean — the tail matters, because the per-user budget in §13.7 is sized against peak-day load).
4. **Compute PEPM COGS at ₹94.43, post-Jan-2027 Flash pricing, across the Lean/Rich blends (§13.12).** This produces a *measured* replacement for the ₹0.15–3.27 band.

**The decision rule (what the measurement gates):**

| Measured tokens vs estimate | Consequence | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ≤ ~1.5× estimate | Model holds comfortably; 93–99% margin intact | Proceed; free bundling safe across the band |
| ~1.5–3× estimate | Low-end (₹50 ARPU) margin compresses but survives | Proceed; bias routing Lean; tighten A1 retrieval |
| ~3–5× estimate | Low-end free-bundling under pressure | Beachhead floor moves up (lean 50–200, not 20–200); metered SKUs carry more |
| > 5× estimate | Free bundling breaks at the low end (§20 item V-04 kill) | Re-price, move the floor, or make A4/A5 revenue load-bearing |

**Why this must precede the financial model.** The margin envelope (§13.6), the FX sensitivity (§13.12), and the competitive-moat argument (§13.14) all rest on the token figure being within ~5× of the estimate. Putting any absolute AI COGS number into a fundraising or pricing model before this measurement is exactly the round-one optimism-bias failure the PRD front matter warns against — a confident number generated with no empirical basis. Instrument first; model second.

**The one number that decides the thesis:** actual tokens-per-employee-month against a real corpus (§20 item V-04). Everything else in this section is either [Verified] (the ratios, the rules, the FX proportionality) or downstream of that single measurement. Instrument it before any AI figure enters a financial model.

## 14. Data Model, Entities & Retention

The data model is where this product's central thesis becomes a schema. If **the filing, not the payslip, is the unit of delivery** (§04, §08 **[Verified]**), then `Filing` is a first-class entity with its own lifecycle, acknowledgement and evidence — not a report generated off a pay run and forgotten. If the 50% wage add-back (Code on Wages s.2(y) / Code on Social Security s.2(88)) creates **two wage bases on one payslip** (§06.9 **[Verified]**), then the schema cannot carry a single `wage` column. And if state rules under the four Labour Codes notify unevenly (§20 **[Verified]**), then rate/slab/definition storage must be **effective-dated and per-jurisdiction from v1**, not retrofitted when the first multi-state customer complains.

This section specifies the conceptual and logical data model — entities, relationships, keys, cardinality — plus the three things a payroll data model in India lives or dies on: **effective-dated (bitemporal) storage**, **multi-state rule storage**, and a **data-classification / retention / deletion regime that reconciles DPDP erasure rights against statutory retention duties.** It is a logical model, not a physical schema (no DDL, per the PRD-only constraint); §15 (System Architecture) maps it onto tenancy and storage.

Three conventions used throughout:

- **Entity names** are `PascalCase`; **fields** are `snake_case`; identifiers ending `_id` are internal surrogate keys, identifiers ending `_no` / `_code` are **external government-issued keys with their own format rules** (UAN, PAN, ESI IP, TAN, PF code) that a filing will reject if malformed (see §14.9).
- **Effective-dated** means the row carries `effective_from` / `effective_to` (business-time validity) *and* `recorded_at` / `superseded_at` (system-time / knowledge-time). The distinction is not academic — see §14.6.
- **Acceptance criteria** are stated in `Given / When / Then` form and numbered `AC-DM-nn`; they are the testable contract a physical schema and its access layer must satisfy. They are gathered per-entity where they bite, and are the hooks §20 (Validation Plan) will exercise.

---

### 14.1 Design principles (the invariants the schema must not violate)

These generalise the payroll-engine invariants (§08.1) to the whole data model. Every entity below is designed to these; they are stated once here rather than repeated per-entity.

| # | Principle | Why it is a schema-level invariant, not a feature | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | **Filing is a first-class entity with lifecycle and evidence** | The product's headline metric is "return filed on time and accepted." A filing must persist its generated artefact, portal acknowledgement, challan/UTR, rejection reasons and the exact input snapshot it was built from. | §04, §08 **[Verified]** |
| D2 | **Bitemporal: business-time and knowledge-time are separate axes** | A March correction filed in September must recompute against March's rules (business time) while recording *when we learned* of the correction (knowledge time). Single-date effective-dating cannot represent "what did we believe in April about March." | §06.9 **[Verified]** |
| D3 | **Rules are data, not code** — every rate, slab, ceiling, definition is a row in `EffectiveDatedRule`, keyed by jurisdiction + effective date | 50% add-back is "or such other per cent as may be notified"; ₹15,000 PF ceiling, ₹21,000 ESI ceiling, state PT slabs, LWF schedules all change by notification. A code deploy per notification is an operating-model failure (§06). | §06.9, §06 **[Verified]** |
| D4 | **Every monetary/statutory field has an immutable audit lineage** — (input × rule_version × formula) → output, with actor, timestamp (NTP-synced), and checker | Required for the four statutory registers (5-yr retention), CA read-only audit, DPDP grievance, and dispute defence. A wrong payroll number is a legal problem. | §06.10, §07, §17 **[Verified]** |
| D5 | **Tenant is the top partition key on every business row** | Multi-tenant SaaS serving regulated buyers (RBI right-to-audit, no turnover threshold) means tenant isolation is a data-model property, not only an app-layer check. | §17, §15 **[Verified]** |
| D6 | **External government keys are validated to source format at write time, and their linkage state is stored, not just the value** | Aadhaar–UAN *seeding status* gates ECR acceptance; PAN *availability* drives s.206AA higher-rate TDS; bank *verification status* gates disbursal. The state is as load-bearing as the value. | §07.1.1, §14.9 **[Verified]** |
| D7 | **PII/sensitive/regulated fields carry a classification tag that drives encryption, masking, access, residency and retention** | DPDP + CERT-In + sectoral (RBI/IRDAI) obligations differ by field. Classification cannot be a wiki page; it must be attached to the field so policy is enforceable and auditable. | §14.5, §17 **[Verified]** |
| D8 | **Delete is a policy engine, not a `DELETE` statement** — DPDP erasure, statutory minimum-retention and litigation-hold contend for the same row | DPDP s.8(7) requires erasure on purpose-completion/withdrawal *unless retention is required by law*; the Codes/IT Act/EPF/ESI mandate multi-year retention. The winner is per-field and time-dependent. | §14.7 **[Verified]** |
| D9 | **Money-of-record and attach/benefit money are two ledgers that never blend** | A benefit wallet, insurance endorsement or interchange event must never silently alter a filed statutory figure. The "two lines never blended" GTM rule (§11 **[Verified]**) is enforced structurally, not just in the P&L slide. | §11 **[Verified]** |

**AC-DM-01** — *Given* any business row (Ring 1–3), *When* it is read or written through any interface (app, API, MCP tool, migration importer, admin console), *Then* the query must be scoped by `tenant_id` and a cross-tenant read must be structurally impossible, not merely filtered (D5).

**AC-DM-02** — *Given* any monetary or statutory field on a `PayrollResult` or `Filing`, *When* its value is inspected, *Then* the exact `(input rows, rule_id versions, formula id, actor, checker, NTP timestamp)` that produced it must be resolvable without recomputation (D4).

---

### 14.2 Entity catalogue

The model has **four rings**: (1) tenancy & org, (2) people & the compliance master, (3) the operating record (comp, attendance, pay, filing), and (4) the cross-cutting spine (rules, documents, audit, consent). Ring 4 entities are referenced by almost everything. The rings are a dependency ordering, not just a grouping: a Ring-3 row is meaningless without its Ring-1/2 parents and its Ring-4 lineage, which is why migration (§14.4.10) imports **outside-in**.



**Figure 87. Data Model Rings**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph R1["Ring 1 - Tenancy &amp; Org"]
    direction LR
    Tenant["Tenant"]
    Employer["Employer / LegalEntity<br/>(PAN, TAN)"]
    Estab["Establishment<br/>(EPF/ESI/PT/LWF/S&amp;E codes)"]
    OrgDim["Dept / CostCentre /<br/>Location(work-state) / Grade"]
    Tenant --> Employer --> Estab
    Estab -.-> OrgDim
  end

  subgraph R2["Ring 2 - People &amp; Compliance Master"]
    direction LR
    Person["Employee / Person<br/>(immutable id)"]
    Employment["Employment<br/>(DOJ to DOL)"]
    StatId["StatutoryIdentifier<br/>(UAN, PAN, ESI IP, PF Member ID)"]
    Elig["EligibilityState<br/>(PF/ESI/PT/gratuity, effective-dated)"]
    Person --> Employment
    Employment --> StatId
    Employment --> Elig
  end

  subgraph R3["Ring 3 - Operating Record (comp, attendance, pay, filing)"]
    direction LR
    Comp["CompensationStructure /<br/>PayComponent / Assignment"]
    Att["AttendanceRecord /<br/>Leave (Policy/Balance/Txn)"]
    PayRun["PayRun"]
    Result["PayrollResult<br/>(rule-versioned)"]

    Filing["Filing<br/>THE UNIT OF DELIVERY"]
    Challan["Challan / Payment"]
    Comp --> PayRun
    Att --> PayRun
    PayRun --> Result --> Payslip
    Result --> Filing
    Filing --> Challan
  end

  subgraph R4["Ring 4 - Cross-cutting Spine (referenced by almost everything)"]
    direction LR
    Rule["EffectiveDatedRule /<br/>Jurisdiction (rules-as-data)"]
    Doc["Document<br/>(classification + retention)"]
    Audit["AuditEvent<br/>(append-only lineage)"]

    Hold["RetentionHold"]
  end

  R1 ==>|"parents"| R2
  R2 ==>|"parents"| R3
  R4 -.->|"lineage / rules / evidence"| R3
  R4 -.-> R2

  Migrate["Migration imports OUTSIDE-IN:<br/>Ring 1 to 2 to 3, spine 4 first"]
  Migrate -.-> R1
```


| Entity | Ring | Purpose | Owns / keyed by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Tenant** | 1 | The paying customer account; top isolation boundary. | `tenant_id` |
| **Employer (LegalEntity)** | 1 | A registered legal employer (company/LLP/firm) under one PAN/TAN. A Tenant may hold several. | `employer_id`, `pan`, `tan` |
| **Establishment** | 1 | A registered place/unit of employment — the unit EPF/ESI/PT/S&E registrations attach to. Per-state, per-code. | `establishment_id`, `epf_code`, `esi_code`, `pt_reg_no`, `lwf_reg_no`, `se_reg_no` |
| **Department / CostCentre / Location / Grade** | 1 | Org dimensions; `Location` carries the **work-location state** that drives PT/LWF/state rules. | `*_id` |
| **Employee (Person)** | 2 | Canonical, immutable-lineage person record across rehire/transfer. | `employee_id` (internal, immutable) |
| **Employment (Engagement)** | 2 | A single employment instance: DOJ→DOL, type, establishment mapping. One Person → many Employments (rehire, inter-entity transfer). | `employment_id` |
| **StatutoryIdentifier** | 2 | Typed external IDs with linkage state (UAN+seeding, PAN, ESI IP, Aadhaar-masked, PRAN, bank+penny-drop). | `stat_id_id`, (`type`, `value`) |
| **EligibilityState** | 2 | Effective-dated *derived* flags (PF/ESI/PT/LWF/gratuity applicability). Computed, never typed. | `eligibility_id` |
| **CompensationStructure** | 3 | A template of ordered `PayComponent`s. | `structure_id` |
| **PayComponent** | 3 | One earning/deduction/reimbursement/statutory/employer-cost line with basis + statutory-inclusion flags (pf/esi/gratuity/pow). | `component_id` |
| **CompensationAssignment** | 3 | Effective-dated binding of an Employment to a structure + component values (CTC revision = new version). | `comp_assign_id` |
| **AttendanceRecord** | 3 | Per-day/per-punch fact; source-tagged (device/geo/mobile/kiosk). | `attendance_id` |
| **LeavePolicy / LeaveBalance / LeaveTransaction** | 3 | Policy, running balance, and the ledger that moves it. | `*_id` |
| **PayRun** | 3 | A period's payroll execution for an Establishment (regular / off-cycle / arrears / bonus / FnF). | `payrun_id` |
| **PayrollResult** | 3 | Per-employee-per-run computed facts, each stamped with the `rule_version` that produced it. | `result_id` |
| **Payslip** | 3 | The rendered artefact off a `PayrollResult` (a document, not the source of truth). | `payslip_id` |
| **Filing** | 3 | **The unit of delivery.** A statutory submission (ECR, ESI challan, PT return, Form 138, Form 130, LWF, register) with lifecycle + acknowledgement + evidence. | `filing_id` |
| **Challan / Payment** | 3 | The money-movement leg of a filing (PF/ESI/PT/TDS challan, CRN, UTR, bank NEFT file). | `challan_id` |
| **EffectiveDatedRule** | 4 | Rates/slabs/ceilings/definitions per jurisdiction per effective window. Rules-as-data. | `rule_id`, (`rule_type`, `jurisdiction`, `effective_from`) |
| **Jurisdiction** | 4 | Central + each State/UT (+ PT local bodies where sub-state, e.g. Maharashtra, Karnataka municipal LWF nuances). | `jurisdiction_id` |
| **Document** | 4 | Any stored file (appointment letter, Form 130, proofs, KYC, register export) with classification + retention class. | `document_id` |
| **ConsentGrant / DataPrincipalRequest** | 4 | DPDP artefacts: notice/consent (where used), and access/correction/erasure/grievance requests. | `consent_id`, `dpr_id` |
| **AuditEvent** | 4 | Immutable who/what/when/before/after/authority/rule_version for every statutory or monetary change. | `audit_id` |
| **RetentionHold** | 4 | Litigation / investigation / dispute hold that suspends deletion on named rows. | `hold_id` |
